Sheet 1 / 11 · Unit 2a–2b · Competitions

Aims of the lesson & Lead-in

Aims of the lesson

By the end of the four periods, you will be able to:

📚Remember · Understand
  • Name the words and chunks of the 4 groups: sport and competitions, crazy competitions and rules, sportspeople, and winning, losing and opinions.
  • Explain what must, have to, can, don’t have to, mustn’t and can’t tell you about a rule: obligatory, allowed, not necessary or not allowed.
  • Recognise how -er, -ist and player turn a sport into a person (golfer, cyclist, chess player) and how compete grows into competitor, competition, competitive.
🛠️Apply · Analyse
  • Use the -ing form in its three jobs: as the subject, after a preposition (good at, afraid of) and after love, hate, enjoy, don’t mind.
  • Find rules, facts and opinions in the article Crazy competitions!, in Tracks 9–12 and in the PET Reading and Listening extras.
  • Compare the arguments for and against competitive sport in schools, and decide which speaker on Track 11 is closest to your own view.
💡Evaluate · Create
  • Describe and evaluate, with the 7-step frame, your favourite sport (Topic 4) or a game many people play in Việt Nam (Topic 6).
  • Upgrade a basic sentence on a common topic level by level, from Level 1 (basic) through Level 2 (detail) to Level 3 (a clause), and try Level 4 (academic).
  • Value teamwork and fair play, on the sports field and in pair and group work in class.

Lead-in 1 · Swimmers, shopping carts and champions: look, guess and react

3:00Choose one photo each, ask your partner its three questions, then change roles.
A sea full of arms
  1. Question 1
    ‘Describe what you can see: the water, the caps and the arms. Roughly how many swimmers are there?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘Is this a race or a swim for fun? What in the photo tells you?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘How far can you swim without stopping, and where did you learn?’
Model answer

The sea is bright blue and full of white splashes, and nearly everyone has a pink or a white cap on. I’d say there are at least two hundred swimmers, all heading the same way at the same moment, so it has to be the start of a race. I learned to swim in the river near my grandparents’ house when I was nine, and these days I can manage about four hundred metres in a pool before I need a rest.

A giant foot on wheels
  1. Question 1
    ‘What are these people pushing, and what is lying on top of it?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘This is a race between teams. What do you think the rules are?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘If your class entered this race, how would you decorate your cart?’
Model answer

They’re pushing an ordinary supermarket cart, and on top of it there’s an enormous plastic leg with a bare foot. My guess is that each team needs one cart, and maybe you’re out if it falls apart before the end. Our class would turn ours into a giant syringe, since we’re all going to be doctors anyway.

Head to toe in mud
  1. Question 1
    ‘Describe the player: his hair, his face, his clothes and what he is holding.’
  2. Question 2
    ‘What game do you think he is playing? Why is everyone so dirty?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Have you ever played a game in heavy rain or mud? How did it end?’
Model answer

His hair is in long dreadlocks, his face is screwed up, and his vest is so muddy you can hardly read the letters on it. He’s carrying an oval ball, so it looks like American football, played on purpose in a field that someone has turned into a swamp. After a heavy storm a few weeks ago we kicked a ball around the training ground, and by the end nobody could tell which team anyone was on.

Four beards on stage
  1. Question 1
    ‘Describe the four men: their clothes, their hats and their beards.’
  2. Question 2
    ‘What do you think the judges are looking for in this competition?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Which man would you give the prize to, and why?’
Model answer

The man on the left looks like a snowman in his white suit and grey top hat, and the one in pink has a cowboy hat to match his suit. I imagine the judges look at the size and shape of each beard, but also at how well the clothes go with it. I’d pick the man on the right, because his moustache curls up at both ends like two perfect snail shells.

Smiling at full speed
  1. Question 1
    ‘Describe the runner: his clothes, his body and his face.’
  2. Question 2
    ‘He is looking sideways and smiling in the middle of a race. What does that tell you about him?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Who is the fastest runner you know? Have you ever raced against them?’
Model answer

He’s in a yellow vest with green down the sides, the name on his chest says BOLT, and you can see every muscle in his arms and legs. A sprinter who smiles sideways halfway through a race must be pretty sure he’s winning, or he’s simply having the time of his life. The fastest runner I know is my roommate, who beat me by about thirty metres in a 400-metre run during our first week at the academy.

A silver plate above her head
  1. Question 1
    ‘Describe the player, her clothes and the trophy. Where do you think she is?’
  2. Question 2
    ‘How do you think she feels at this moment? How can you tell?’
  3. Question 3
    ‘Have you ever gone up on a stage to collect something? What was it for?’
Model answer

She’s dressed completely in white, with white wristbands, and she’s lifting a huge round silver plate covered in patterns. With a crowd behind her and a smile that big, I think she’s just won a major tennis final. The only time I’ve gone up on a stage to collect anything was in grade 11, when I came second in a provincial biology contest and walked off with a set of anatomy books.

Lead-in 2 · Winning, rules and sport: agree or disagree?

4:00Choose a side, then give one reason and one real example from your own life.

1 · Winning is the most important thing in sport.

Model answer

I disagree. In my first year at high school our volleyball team lost every single match, and those Saturday mornings are still some of my happiest memories. You find out a lot more about your friends when you’re losing together.

2 · Crazy competitions are a waste of time and money.

Model answer

Not at all. Last month our dormitory held a race where each team carried a full bucket of water across the yard on a stretcher, and I hadn’t laughed that hard in months. It cost us nothing but a few buckets, and it got people talking who had never said a word to each other before.

3 · Every school should have a competitive sports day.

Model answer

Only if it isn’t just a show for the stars. On sports day at my old school, the same six runners raced in every final while the rest of us sat on the steps in the heat for three hours with nothing to do. If a sports day is really for the whole school, then the whole school has to get a chance to compete.

4 · Watching sport on TV is as good as playing it.

Model answer

I don’t think so. Watching a big match with friends on a Sunday afternoon is great fun, but my heart rate hardly changes. A twenty-minute jog round the parade ground does far more for my body than ninety minutes on the sofa.

5 · Strict rules make a game more fun, not less.

Model answer

I agree, up to a point. When we play basketball after class with nobody to referee, almost every game ends in an argument about fouls. Clear rules mean you can stop shouting at each other and actually play.

6 · Doctors should do sport to set an example for their patients.

Model answer

I’d agree. A doctor who tells you to exercise and then gets out of breath on one flight of stairs isn’t very convincing. My uncle is a surgeon who cycles eight kilometres to the hospital every morning, and his patients are always asking him how he finds the energy.

Useful language
  • I’d go along with that, because …
  • That works for …, but it doesn’t work for …
  • From my own experience, …
  • I’m not so sure. For example, …
  • It really comes down to …

Lead-in 3 · Listen · Track 9 · The Ironman

6:00Read the six questions first, listen twice, then talk about the photo with a partner.
Track 9

Listen to someone talking about the photo and choose the best answer (SB p. 21 Ex 2)

Played 0×
Transcript · Audioscript 9

An Ironman competition has three different races. In the swimming race, the competitors swim for 3.86 kilometres. Then they cycle for 180 kilometres, and finally they run a marathon at the end. The world final of the Ironman Championship is in Hawaii and it’s very competitive. Every year, around one thousand, nine hundred people compete against each other in front of thousands of spectators.

1In what order do the competitors do the three races?
Listen for the order words. The speaker starts with “In the swimming race …”, goes on with “Then they cycle …” and ends with “finally they run a marathon at the end”. Then and finally fix the order: swim, cycle, run.
2For which race does the speaker NOT give a distance in kilometres?
He gives two numbers: 3.86 kilometres for the swim and 180 kilometres for the bike ride. For the last race he only says “they run a marathon”, because a marathon is already a fixed distance that listeners are expected to know.
3A marathon is about 42 kilometres. Roughly how far does an Ironman competitor travel from the start to the finish?
Add the three parts: 3.86 km (swim) + 180 km (bike) + about 42 km (marathon) ≈ 226 km. B leaves out the marathon, C leaves out the bike ride, and 1,900 (E) is the number of people at the world final, not a distance.
4‘The world final of the Ironman Championship is in Hawaii and it’s very competitive.’ What does it refer to?
It points back to the subject of the same sentence, “the world final of the Ironman Championship”. A final is competitive because the strongest athletes all want to win it; an island (C) cannot be competitive, and the crowd (D) only comes in the next sentence.
5Which sentence matches what the speaker says about the people at the world final?
“Around one thousand, nine hundred people compete against each other in front of thousands of spectators.” Compete = take part in the race; spectators = the people who watch. A swaps the two groups round, and nothing in the recording mentions separate days (E).
6What picture of the Ironman does the speaker give us?
Every detail builds the same picture: three races, 3.86 km in the water, 180 km on a bike, a whole marathon, a world final that is “very competitive” and “thousands of spectators”. The speaker never talks about danger (B), and a marathon is anything but a short run (E).
SB p. 21 Ex 1 · Look at the photo again, then tell the class
  1. What sport is it? Which of the three Ironman races does the photo show?
  2. Do you like this kind of sport? Why? / Why not?
Model answer · question 1

It’s a triathlon, and the photo shows the first of the three races, the swim, so everyone is still bunched together in one enormous crowd. The caption in the coursebook says these athletes are in the sea at Cozumel, in Mexico, fighting for a place in the Ironman championship.

Model answer · question 2

I like watching it more than doing it. On a good day I can run ten kilometres, but swimming in the open sea with hundreds of elbows flying past my head sounds terrifying. One day I might try a short triathlon, just not this one.

Useful language
  • It looks like … to me.
  • What I like about it is …
  • I’d rather watch it than …, because …
  • I could never …, but I’d like to try …

Sheet 2 / 11 · Unit 2a–2b · 4 periods

Roadmap

1 · Learning outcomes

Reading · SB p. 22 + PET Parts 2–4
  • Crazy competitions! (listen and read, Track 10) and three PET texts
  • Rules, details, reference words and the writer’s purpose
  • Reading A: at least 9 of the 12 questions right
  • Each PET part: at least 4 of 5
Listening · Tracks 11–12 + PET Parts 1, 3, 4
  • Listening A: three speakers on competitive sport in schools, for and against
  • Listening B: What’s on TV?, a short chat about the Tour de France full of -ing forms
  • PET: seven short extracts, a talk about the academy’s Spring Sports Festival, a radio interview with a young doctor who does triathlons
  • Listening A: 7 of 10 or more · Listening B: 4 of 6 or more
  • PET Part 1: 5 of 7 or more · Parts 3 and 4: 4 of 6 or more
Speaking · Parts 1–3
  • Part 1: about 30 seconds per answer (Point → Why → Example), using at least one Sheet 4 chunk
  • Part 2: two minutes on card A (Topic 4, your favourite sport) or card B (Topic 6, a popular game in your country)
  • Part 3: a one-minute answer that uses all seven steps of the frame
  • Sheet 11: two 20-second answers, on the rules of a game you play with friends and on whether winning matters to you
Writing · upgrading a sentence
  • Level 1: a correct core in every sentence, a subject + a finite verb
  • Level 2: precise details (who, what kind, where, when, how often) in the right order
  • Level 3: a reason or result clause (because / , so / , which) with the right comma; no fragments, run-ons or comma splices
  • Level 4 (optional): a noun phrase in place of the action, plus a careful verb such as may
  • Final task: two sentences of your own, each upgraded to Level 3, or Level 4 if you can
Grammar
  • Verbs for rules: must / have to (obligatory), can (allowed), don’t have to (not necessary), mustn’t / can’t (not allowed)
  • mustn’t and don’t have to kept apart: their meanings are very different
  • -ing forms in three places: at the start of a sentence (Swimming is …), after at, of, about, with, and after verbs of liking and disliking
  • About 80% or more of the items right in Exercises 7–15
Vocabulary
  • Chunks from all four groups in your spoken answers and your sentences
  • Names for sportspeople with -er, -ist and player; the family compete, competitor, competition, competitive
  • At least 13 of the 16 chunks in the Sheet 10 quiz one week later
  • Exercises 1–6: roughly four answers in five correct, or better

4 · How to learn a group of words

1

Read the Core aloud

  • Begin with the words you wrote in Lead-in 4
  • Mark the stress as you go: comPETitor, compeTItion
2

Choose 5 Advanced words

  • The five you would need to explain the rules of your favourite sport
  • Keep the others for the following week
3

Hide and recall

  • Cover the meaning line and explain the word in English
  • Cover the word and find it again from its meaning
4

Write one true sentence

  • About something you really play at the academy, from chess to football
  • Use a rule verb: have to, can or mustn’t
5

Talk for 30 seconds

  • Read your sentence aloud and add two more with an -ing form
  • Start with I really enjoy … or I’m quite good at …
Sheet 3 / 11 · 4 vocabulary groups · Crazy competitions! & Winning and losing

Vocabulary: sport and competitions, rules, sportspeople and opinions about sport

Group 1 · Sport and competitions: races, matches and results

Core
Events and people
a competition /ˌkɒmpəˈtɪʃn/
an organised event in which people try to do better than everyone else and win something
Our company entered a first-aid competition against five other units and came second.
a race /reɪs/
a contest to see who can get from the start to the end the fastest
The 3 km race around the parade ground starts at six, before the sun gets too hot.
a match /mætʃ/
a game in which two players or two teams play against each other
After the last lecture, Year 1 and Year 2 played a football match that ended just as it got dark.
a championship /ˈtʃæmpiənʃɪp/
a series of games or races that decides who is the best in a sport
Our volleyball team reached the semi-finals of the inter-university championship last spring.
a final /ˈfaɪnl/
the last game of a contest, which decides the winner
Half the dormitory stayed up past midnight to watch the final on a laptop in the corridor.
a team /tiːm/
a group of people who play or work together on the same side
Every team in the relay needs four runners and one reserve.
a player /ˈpleɪə(r)/
a person who takes part in a game or a sport
Our best basketball player is only 1 m 70, but nobody can stop her near the basket.
a competitor /kəmˈpetɪtə(r)/
a person who takes part in a race or contest
Each competitor in the swimming event gets a number written on their arm in black pen.
a spectator /spekˈteɪtə(r)/
a person who watches a sports event without taking part
On the day of the cross-country run, the spectators sat under the trees because the stand had no roof.
a referee /ˌrefəˈriː/
the official who watches a game and makes sure everyone plays fairly
When a player went down holding his knee, the referee waved our medical team onto the pitch.
a fan /fæn/
a person who loves a sport, a club or a sports star very much
My grandfather has followed the same football club for fifty years and still calls himself its biggest fan.
Winning and scoring
win /wɪn/
come first in a game, race or contest
Nam's platoon won the obstacle course by four seconds and celebrated with iced tea.
lose /luːz/
not succeed in a game; be beaten
We lost 3–2 to the Year 3 team, but it was the best game of the term.
a winner /ˈwɪnə(r)/
the person or team that comes first
The winner of the chess tournament gets two free tickets to the cinema.
a goal /ɡəʊl/
a point you get when the ball goes into the net, in games such as football or hockey
Tuấn's goal in the last minute sent the whole bench running onto the pitch.
score (v) /skɔː(r)/
get a point or a goal in a game
She scored twelve points in the first set alone.
a point /pɔɪnt/
one unit that you add to your total in a game, a quiz or a test
Each correct answer in the quiz was worth one point, and we lost by just two.
a medal /ˈmedl/
a flat, round piece of metal given to someone for winning or for doing very well
Every cadet who completed the night march got a small bronze medal on a red ribbon.
a prize /praɪz/
something valuable, such as money or a cup, given to the person who wins
First prize in the photo contest was a weekend pass and a new pair of trainers.
the finish line /ðə ˈfɪnɪʃ laɪn/
the place where a race ends, often a painted mark or a tape
Two nurses waited at the finish line with water and ice packs for the slower runners.
beat (someone) /biːt/
defeat a person or a team in a game
The first-year team beat the fourth-years 4–1, and nobody let the older students forget it.
Advanced
Bigger events and results
a tournament/ˈtʊənəmənt/a contest with many players or teams, who play a series of games until only one is leftSixteen faculties signed up for the five-a-side tournament, so the games ran over three weekends.
a triathlon/traɪˈæθlən/a race in which people swim, then cycle, then run, one straight after the otherAn Olympic-distance triathlon is a 1.5 km swim, a 40 km bike ride and a 10 km run.
an opponent/əˈpəʊnənt/the person or team you play againstMy opponent in the final was left-handed, and her serves kept curling away from me.
a draw/drɔː/a game that ends with both sides on the same scoreThe match ended in a 1–1 draw, so the two captains agreed to settle it with penalties.
qualify/ˈkwɒlɪfaɪ/reach the standard you need to go through to a later roundOnly the top three runners in each heat qualify for Sunday's final.
a trophy/ˈtrəʊfi/a cup, plate or small statue given to the winner of a contestThe faculty's football trophy has sat in our commander's office for two years now.
Collocations
Talking about a race or a match
score a goal/ˌskɔːr ə ˈɡəʊl/get the ball past the keeper and into the netNobody expected the shy new cadet to score a goal in his first game, least of all himself.
win a race/ˌwɪn ə ˈreɪs/come first when people compete to be fastestMy little sister won a race at her primary school and talked about nothing else for a week.
cross the finish line/ˌkrɒs ðə ˈfɪnɪʃ laɪn/complete a race by passing the last mark on the coursePhúc crossed the finish line holding his side, then lay flat on the grass for ten minutes.
compete against/kəmˈpiːt əˈɡenst/try to beat another person or team in a contestThis year our volleyball team will compete against the nursing school for the first time.
win a gold medal/ˌwɪn ə ˌɡəʊld ˈmedl/come first in a big event, such as the Olympics, and receive the top awardHer dream is to win a gold medal at the national student games before she graduates.
cheer (someone) on/ˌtʃɪə(r) ˈɒn/shout and clap to encourage a player or a team during a gameHalf our platoon came to cheer us on in the volleyball semi-final, banging plastic water bottles together.

Group 2 · Crazy competitions and rules

Core
The competitions
crazy /ˈkreɪzi/
very strange or silly, often in a funny way
My roommate had the crazy idea of carrying a watermelon all the way round the 5 km route.
annual /ˈænjuəl/
happening once every year
My hometown holds an annual boat race on the river, and the whole town comes out to watch.
a shopping cart /ˈʃɒpɪŋ kɑːt/
a large metal basket on wheels that you push round a supermarket (British English: a trolley)
In the Idiotarod, teams of five pull a shopping cart through the streets of New York.
decorate /ˈdekəreɪt/
make something look more attractive by adding pictures, colours or objects
We decorated our platoon's flag with a red cross and the names of all twelve members.
wheels /wiːlz/
the round parts under a car, a bike or a trolley that turn so that it can move
One of the wheels on the stretcher trolley kept squeaking, so the porter oiled it.
mud /mʌd/
soft, wet earth
After the night exercise in the rain, our boots were so heavy with mud that we left them outside the dormitory.
a field /fiːld/
an open area of grass where people play sports
The football field behind the gym turns into a pond every time it rains for more than an hour.
a beard /bɪəd/
hair that grows on a man's chin and cheeks
Our old anatomy lecturer has had the same white beard for as long as anyone can remember.
a moustache /məˈstɑːʃ/
hair that grows above a man's top lip
The old surgeon twisted the ends of his grey moustache whenever he was thinking hard.
a category /ˈkætəɡəri/
a group of people or things of the same type, for example in a contest
The photo contest has three categories: people, nature and life at the academy.
enter (a competition) /ˈentə(r)/
officially join a contest by adding your name to the list
Thảo entered the poetry contest at the last minute and still came second.
The rules
a rule /ruːl/
an instruction that tells you what you must or must not do in a game or a place
The most important rule in the lab is simple: no food and no drink, ever.
obligatory /əˈblɪɡətri/
required by the regulations, so you have no choice
Helmets are obligatory for every rider in the campus bike race.
allowed /əˈlaʊd/
OK to do, because the regulations say you may
Phones are allowed in the library, but only on silent.
not allowed /ˌnɒt əˈlaʊd/
against the regulations, so you may not do it
Running beside the pool is not allowed, and the lifeguard blows her whistle at anyone who tries.
at the end of sixty minutes /ət ði ˌend əv ˌsɪksti ˈmɪnɪts/
when one hour is over
At the end of sixty minutes, the quiz master collected the papers, finished or not.
be over eighteen /bi ˌəʊvər eɪˈtiːn/
be older than 18
Anyone who wants a place on the boxing course at the city gym needs to be over eighteen.
a time limit /ˈtaɪm lɪmɪt/
the longest period you are given to finish something
There's a two-minute time limit for each station in the first-aid test, so work fast but carefully.
argue (with) /ˈɑːɡjuː/
speak angrily to someone because you disagree
My brother argued with the umpire about one line call and then lost the next five points.
break the rules /ˌbreɪk ðə ˈruːlz/
do something that the regulations say you must not do
Anyone caught checking a phone during the quiz breaks the rules and loses all their points.
send off /ˌsend ˈɒf/
(of a referee) make a player leave the game and not come back
The referee sent our defender off for a second yellow card, so we played the last twenty minutes with ten men.
false /fɔːls/
not real, but made to look real
The actor in the training video wore a false nose and fake blood to play the injured soldier.
similar to /ˈsɪmələ tə/
almost the same as
Beach volleyball is similar to the indoor game, but each side has only two players.
Advanced
Stricter rules
compulsory/kəmˈpʌlsəri/that you must do because a law or an official says soIn our first year, morning exercise was compulsory, even on the coldest days of January.
forbidden/fəˈbɪdn/not allowed at all; bannedUsing a phone during the anatomy exam is strictly forbidden.
permitted/pəˈmɪtɪd/allowed, especially by an official rule (formal)Visitors are permitted on the ward between four and seven in the evening.
disqualify/dɪsˈkwɒlɪfaɪ/remove someone from a contest because they have broken a ruleThe judges disqualified the fastest boat for steering into the next lane.
an entry fee/ˈentri fiː/the money you pay to take part in an eventThe chess club charges a small entry fee to pay for the prizes and the tea.
a penalty/ˈpenəlti/a punishment for breaking a rule in a game, often a free shot at goalHe missed the penalty, and the goalkeeper didn't even have to move.
Collocations
Rules for a crazy competition
enter a competition/ˌentər ə ˌkɒmpəˈtɪʃn/sign up so that you can take part in an eventIf you want to enter a competition like the Idiotarod, the first thing you need is four very patient friends.
follow the rules/ˌfɒləʊ ðə ˈruːlz/do what the regulations sayA player who follows the rules and loses earns more respect than one who cheats and wins.
in fancy dress/ɪn ˌfænsi ˈdres/wearing a funny costume, for example as an animal or a cartoon characterMany teams in the Idiotarod run in fancy dress, and some decorate their carts to match.
against the rules/əˌɡenst ðə ˈruːlz/not allowed by the regulations of a game or a placeTalking to the cadet next to you during the anatomy test is against the rules, even if you only want to borrow a pen.
take place/ˌteɪk ˈpleɪs/happen at a planned time, as an event or a meeting doesThe academy's swimming championship takes place every June, so the pool is full of cadets all through May.
bend the rules/ˌbend ðə ˈruːlz/change or ignore a regulation a little, usually to help someoneThe coach bent the rules a little and let the injured cadet run the relay in trainers instead of boots.

Group 3 · Sportspeople: the suffixes -er, -ist, player

Core
-er · -ist
a footballer /ˈfʊtbɔːlə(r)/
a person who plays the world's favourite ball game with the feet, often as a job
My cousin trained to be a footballer until a knee injury sent him to medical school instead.
a golfer /ˈɡɒlfə(r)/
a person who hits a small white ball into a series of holes with long clubs
The golfer walked eighteen holes in the heat and barely spoke to anyone.
a runner /ˈrʌnə(r)/
a person who races on foot, or jogs for fun
Every morning at five, a lone runner does laps of the lake near our dormitory.
a swimmer /ˈswɪmə(r)/
a person who moves through water with the arms and legs, especially well or in races
Hà is the strongest swimmer in our class; she grew up in a fishing village and learned before she could read.
a boxer /ˈbɒksə(r)/
a person who fights with closed hands in big padded gloves, as a sport
The boxer came into the clinic with a cut above his eye and a huge smile, because he'd won.
a surfer /ˈsɜːfə(r)/
a person who rides on waves standing on a long board
The surfer waited almost an hour for the right wave, then rode it for about five seconds.
a cyclist /ˈsaɪklɪst/
a person who rides a bike
A cyclist in a bright yellow jacket is much easier for drivers to see at night.
a motorcyclist /ˈməʊtəsaɪklɪst/
a person who rides a motorbike
On the ward we met a motorcyclist who was lucky to be alive because he'd worn a good helmet.
a gymnast /ˈdʒɪmnæst/
a person who performs exercises on bars, beams and mats that need strength and balance
The young gymnast landed perfectly, then limped off the mat holding her ankle.
an athlete /ˈæθliːt/
a person who is good at sports, especially running, jumping and throwing
Doctors at the sports centre check every athlete's heart before the season starts.
… player · other sportspeople
a tennis player /ˈtenɪs pleɪə(r)/
someone who competes in the racket game with a net across a court
As a tennis player, my aunt was never the fastest, but she almost never made a mistake.
a squash player /ˈskwɒʃ pleɪə(r)/
someone who hits a small rubber ball against the walls of a closed court
A good squash player can be soaked with sweat after just twenty minutes on court.
a baseball player /ˈbeɪsbɔːl pleɪə(r)/
someone who takes part in the American game in which batters hit and then run round the four corners of a diamond
Few baseball players are famous in Việt Nam, but in Japan and the USA the best ones are huge stars.
a chess player /ˈtʃes pleɪə(r)/
someone who competes at the board game with kings, queens and pawns
The best chess player in our dormitory plays three games at once and usually wins all of them.
a racing driver /ˈreɪsɪŋ draɪvə(r)/
someone who competes in very fast cars on a circuit
A racing driver needs a strong neck as much as quick reactions.
a champion /ˈtʃæmpiən/
the person or team that has won a contest, especially the most important one
Last year's table tennis champion went out in the first round this time, and took it very well.
a coach /kəʊtʃ/
a person who trains a sportsperson or a team
Our coach makes us run up the stairs of the lecture building whenever we're late for training.
Advanced
Special sportspeople
a sprinter/ˈsprɪntə(r)/a runner who races over short distances at top speedIn 2016 Usain Bolt became the first sprinter to win the Olympic 100 m at three Games in a row, after 2008 and 2012.
a heptathlete/hepˈtæθliːt/a person who competes in seven track and field events held over two daysJessica Ennis-Hill was the British heptathlete who won Olympic gold in front of a home crowd in London in 2012.
a cricketer/ˈkrɪkɪtə(r)/a person who plays the bat-and-ball game loved in England, India and AustraliaHardly anyone in Vietnam plays the game, but in India a top cricketer is more famous than any film star.
a wrestler/ˈreslə(r)/a person who fights by holding and throwing the other person to the ground, as a sportThe wrestler had to lose two kilos in a week to stay in his weight class.
a goalkeeper/ˈɡəʊlkiːpə(r)/the player who guards the net and tries to stop shots going inOur goalkeeper saved two penalties and was carried off the pitch on everyone's shoulders.
a captain/ˈkæptɪn/the leader of a sports teamThe captain called everyone together at half-time and calmly changed the plan.
Collocations
Describing sportspeople
a professional footballer/ə prəˌfeʃənl ˈfʊtbɔːlə(r)/a person who earns a living by kicking a ball for a clubScouts watched Tâm for two seasons, but in the end he wasn't quite good enough to become a professional footballer.
an Olympic champion/ən əˌlɪmpɪk ˈtʃæmpiən/a person who has come first at the summer or winter Games held every four yearsNobody in my village had ever seen an Olympic champion except on TV.
a world-class athlete/ə ˌwɜːld klɑːs ˈæθliːt/a sportsperson who is among the very best on the planetEven a world-class athlete needs rest days, because the body gets stronger while it recovers.
a household name/ə ˌhaʊshəʊld ˈneɪm/a person so famous that almost everyone in the country knows who they areAfter one brilliant season, the young striker became a household name, and his face was on every bus stop in the city.
break a world record/ˌbreɪk ə ˌwɜːld ˈrekɔːd/do better than anyone has ever done beforeNobody in our class will ever break a world record, but we can all beat our own best time.
retire from sport/rɪˌtaɪə frəm ˈspɔːt/give up competing at the end of a career, often because of age or injuryAfter her third knee operation, the volleyball star chose to retire from sport at 29, and now she coaches children.

Group 4 · Winning, losing and opinions about sport

Core
Competitive or not
competitive /kəmˈpetətɪv/
wanting very much to win or to be better than others
Linh is so competitive that she even times herself brushing her teeth.
non-competitive /ˌnɒn kəmˈpetətɪv/
done for fun or health, with no winners or losers
The Saturday walk round the lake is non-competitive, so nobody cares if you stop for a glass of sugarcane juice.
teamwork /ˈtiːmwɜːk/
the way people in a group cooperate to reach a shared aim
The rescue drill went smoothly because of good teamwork, not because anyone was a hero.
physical health /ˌfɪzɪkl ˈhelθ/
the condition of your body: how strong, fit and well it is
Long night shifts can harm your physical health if you never make time to move.
get exercise /ˌɡet ˈeksəsaɪz/
move your body so that you stay fit
I get most of my exercise by climbing the six floors to the anatomy lab every day.
do your best /ˌduː jə ˈbest/
put in all the effort you are able to give
You won't know every answer in the oral exam, so just do your best and stay calm.
try hard /ˌtraɪ ˈhɑːd/
put a lot of effort into something
He wasn't the most talented player, but he tried so hard that the coach picked him every week.
as long as /əz ˈlɒŋ əz/
only if; on condition that
You can borrow my bike as long as you bring it back before roll call.
a sports day /ˈspɔːts deɪ/
an event at a school or college when every student can join races and games
At my primary school's sports day, I signed up for the sack race and fell over twice.
a lesson /ˈlesn/
something you learn from an experience, often a painful one
Losing the final by one point taught us a lesson we still talk about: never relax before the whistle.
Feelings and opinions
enjoy /ɪnˈdʒɔɪ/
get pleasure from something
I really enjoy cycling to the academy on cool mornings, before the traffic gets heavy.
hate /heɪt/
dislike something very much
My roommate hates getting up early, so the 5:30 alarm is a daily battle.
can't stand /ˌkɑːnt ˈstænd/
find something so unpleasant that it is unbearable
I can't stand watching penalty shoot-outs, so I always leave the room.
don't mind /ˌdəʊnt ˈmaɪnd/
be happy enough to do something; it doesn't bother you
Tú doesn't mind cleaning the boots for the whole platoon if someone else makes the tea.
get more exercise /ˌɡet ˌmɔːr ˈeksəsaɪz/
move your body more often than before
Since I started walking to the hospital, I get more exercise without even thinking about it.
shout at /ˈʃaʊt ət/
speak to someone very loudly and angrily
The coach apologised the next day for shouting at the goalkeeper in front of everyone.
be good at /bi ˈɡʊd ət/
have a talent or a skill for something
Quang is good at explaining the rules of any game in under a minute.
be afraid of /bi əˈfreɪd əv/
feel fear about something
As a child, I was afraid of deep water, so I only learned to swim at nineteen.
be bored with /bi ˈbɔːd wɪð/
feel tired of something because it is dull or has gone on too long
After a month of the same drills, the whole squad was bored with practising and wanted a real match.
be worried about /bi ˈwʌrid əˈbaʊt/
feel nervous because something bad might happen
Before the swimming test, Hoa was more worried about the cold water than the distance.
get angry /ˌɡet ˈæŋɡri/
become cross or annoyed
Our coach never shouts, but when he gets angry, he goes very quiet.
boring /ˈbɔːrɪŋ/
dull and not interesting
Some people find golf boring to watch, but my dad can sit through a whole tournament.
exciting /ɪkˈsaɪtɪŋ/
making you feel happy, eager and full of energy
The most exciting moment of the race came in the last fifty metres, when three runners were side by side.
Advanced
The psychology of winning and losing
self-confidence/ˌself ˈkɒnfɪdəns/belief in what you are able to doWinning her first match gave Thu the self-confidence to speak up in class as well.
pressure/ˈpreʃə(r)/the stress of having to do well, often because others expect itThe pressure of playing in front of their own fans made the home side nervous in the first half.
fair play/ˌfeə ˈpleɪ/honest behaviour in sport: respecting the rules and the other sideBoth teams got an award for fair play after a match with no yellow cards at all.
a role model/ˈrəʊl mɒdl/a person others look up to and want to copyFor my younger brother, our neighbour, a sixty-year-old nurse who still plays volleyball every weekend, is the perfect role model.
motivate/ˈməʊtɪveɪt/make someone want to work or try harderNothing motivates our platoon like the chance to beat the cadets in the next building.
a sore loser/ˌsɔː ˈluːzə(r)/someone who behaves badly or complains when they don't winNobody wants to play cards with Đức any more, because he's such a sore loser.
Collocations
Talking about competitive sport
work well in teams/ˌwɜːk ˌwel ɪn ˈtiːmz/cooperate easily with other people in a groupHospitals need doctors who work well in teams, because nobody saves a patient alone.
learn to win and lose/ˌlɜːn tə ˌwɪn ən ˈluːz/find out how to handle both success and failureMy nephew is only six, so he still has to learn to win and lose without throwing the board on the floor.
take defeat well/ˌteɪk dɪˈfiːt ˈwel/accept losing calmly, without complaining or blaming othersOur captain takes defeat well: after the final he shook every opponent's hand and helped them carry their kit to the bus.
take part in/ˌteɪk ˈpɑːt ɪn/join an activity or an eventOver two hundred cadets took part in the cross-country run, including three of our lecturers.
perform under pressure/pəˌfɔːm ˌʌndə ˈpreʃə(r)/do well when a lot depends on you and people are watchingSurgeons, like penalty takers, have to perform under pressure, with everyone in the room watching their hands.
be good for your health/bi ˈɡʊd fə jə ˈhelθ/help the body and mind stay wellMy grandmother insists that a short walk after dinner is good for your health; she hasn't missed one in years.
win at all costs/ˌwɪn ət ˌɔːl ˈkɒsts/be ready to do anything, even cheat, to come firstA coach who teaches children to win at all costs soon has a team that cheats whenever the referee looks away.
a sense of achievement/ə ˌsens əv əˈtʃiːvmənt/the good feeling you get when you have done something difficultFinishing my first 10 km run at dawn gave me a sense of achievement that lasted through the whole exam week.
stay in shape/ˌsteɪ ɪn ˈʃeɪp/keep your body fit and healthy through regular exerciseMy father, a retired army doctor, still stays in shape by swimming a kilometre at the city pool every morning.
Sheet 4 / 11 · Grammar · verbs for rules · the -ing form · the sound /ŋ/ · 30 chunks

Grammar & sentence patterns

1 · Grammar: verbs for rules: must, have to, can, don't have to, mustn't, can't

The grammar box, sentence by sentence (SB p. 23) · more examples from the Grammar summary (SB p. 158)
In the grammar box · SB p. 23What the rule saysThe same meaning · SB p. 158
Each team must have five people and a shopping cart.obligatory · must + bare verbRunners must arrive twenty minutes before the race.
All the teams have to start and finish at the same place.obligatory · have to (has to after he, she, it)You have to train hard to do a marathon.
Players can pick up the ball and run with it.allowed · can + bare verbMembers can use the swimming pool for free.
They don't have to run on the same roads.not obligatory, but allowed · don't + have toYou don't have to be fit to join the club.
They mustn't finish without the cart!not allowed · mustn't = must notYou mustn't leave any bags in this area.
They can't change the wheels.not allowed · can't = cannotYou can't touch the ball in football.
Speaking or a written notice? (SB p. 158)
Spoken English · have to, can'tFormal written English · must, must notSB p. 158
You have to pay $40 to do the race.Competitors must pay $40 to enter the race.obligatory
You can't go near the pool with shoes on.Customers must not go near the pool with shoes on.not allowed

4 · Functions: 10 functions, 30 chunks

1 · Describing a competition

  • It's a race / match between …
  • It takes place every … in …
  • The winner is the team / person who …

It's a race between pairs of cadets carrying a sack of rice, and the winner is the pair who reach the flag first.

2 · Saying what is obligatory

  • You have to … before you …
  • Every player must …
  • It's compulsory to …

Every player must show a medical certificate before the first game of the season.

3 · Saying what is allowed

  • You can … if you want.
  • You're allowed to …
  • It's fine to … as long as …

It's fine to walk part of the route, as long as you stay on the marked path.

4 · Saying what is not necessary

  • You don't have to …
  • There's no need to …
  • It isn't necessary to … unless …

There's no need to bring a racket; the club lends them out for free.

5 · Saying what is not allowed

  • You mustn't … under any circumstances.
  • You can't … during …
  • … is not allowed / is forbidden.

Talking to the other players is not allowed once the chess clock starts.

6 · Asking about the rules

  • Do I have to …?
  • Can I … or do I have to …?
  • What happens if someone …?

What happens if someone drops the baton in the relay?

7 · Saying what you enjoy or hate doing

  • I really enjoy … -ing
  • I can't stand … -ing
  • I don't mind … -ing, but …

I don't mind swimming in cold water, but getting out afterwards is torture.

8 · Saying what you are good at or afraid of

  • I'm quite good at … -ing
  • I've never been very good at …
  • I'm a bit afraid of … -ing

I've never been very good at catching, so naturally they always put me in goal.

9 · Giving an opinion about competitive sport

  • In my view, competition teaches …
  • I'm not convinced that …
  • Winning matters, but …

Winning matters, but learning to lose without sulking matters more.

10 · Agreeing and disagreeing politely

  • I see what you mean, but …
  • That's true up to a point.
  • I couldn't agree more.

That's true up to a point, but some children only start to enjoy sport when nobody is keeping score.

5 · Upgrade your sentences: B1 → B1+ / B2

B1B1+ / B2
We played football and we won.We beat the dentistry cadets 3–1 in the final, and our goalkeeper was the hero of the night.
The race was very hard and many people stopped.Only half of the competitors managed to cross the finish line; the heat and the hills stopped the rest.
There were a lot of people watching.Mỹ Đình Stadium was packed with spectators, and the roar when the home side scored made the stands shake.
You must not argue with the referee.Players who argue with the referee risk a yellow card, and a second one gets them sent off.
It is not necessary to be fast.You don't have to be fast to join; what really matters is that you do your best.
I like swimming very much.I really enjoy swimming, especially early in the morning before the pool gets crowded.
I don't like competitions.I'm not a very competitive person, so I prefer non-competitive games where nobody keeps the score.
My brother plays tennis very well.My brother is such a talented tennis player that he could have turned professional if he hadn't chosen medicine.
Sport is good for health.Regular sport keeps you physically healthy, and the teamwork it takes on the pitch is exactly what we need on the ward.
He is angry when he loses.He's a real sore loser: whenever his side loses, he gets angry with everyone around him.
Many children don't like sport at school.Some children can't stand PE lessons because they are always the last to be picked for a team.
Children learn from winning and losing.Playing in real matches teaches children to cope with defeat as well as victory, which builds self-confidence for later life.

6 · The answer frame: 7 steps, one job each

Sample question: ‘Which sport would you recommend to a busy medical student, and why?’

1Point

Jobanswer the question directly

Ask yourselfWhat is my answer?

I'd tell any busy medical student to take up …

2Why

Jobgive your main reason

Ask yourselfWhy do I think so?

The main reason is that …

3How

Jobexplain how that reason works in real life

Ask yourselfHow does it happen?

It works like this: …

4Example

Jobshow one real case: who, where, when

Ask yourselfWho or what proves it?

Take my classmate …, for example.

5Result

Jobsay what happened in that case

Ask yourselfWhat changed?

About a month later, …

6Limitation

Jobadmit the other side or a problem

Ask yourselfWhat is the weak point?

Admittedly, …

7Evaluation

Jobgive your final view in new words

Ask yourselfSo what do I think now?

Still, … (in new words, not your Point again)

Model answer · each step does its job, all in one paragraph
In the model answers:
  • Point Why … (coloured tags) = the steps of the answer frame, as on the seven cards above
  • frame language = phrases that give an opinion, a reason, an example, a contrast or a conclusion
  • unit vocabulary = words from the four Sheet 3 groups of this lesson

PointHonestly, I'd tell any busy medical student to take up skipping. WhyThe main reason is that you get real exercise in very little time, and time is exactly what we never have. HowIt works like this: a rope fits in your locker, you need only two square metres of floor, and you don't need a team or an opponent, so a quarter of an hour between evening study and lights out is enough to get your heart pumping hard. ExampleTake my classmate Khánh, for example. In our second year he was always out of breath on the stairs, so he started skipping in the dormitory corridor for fifteen minutes after evening study, five nights a week. ResultAbout a month later he could run up the five floors of the lecture building without stopping, and he said he was sleeping better too, even in the week before the anatomy exam. LimitationAdmittedly, it gets boring fast, and the cadets in the room below won't thank you for the noise. EvaluationStill, when your days are long and you never know when they'll end, a sport you can fit into a quarter of an hour, on your own, does more for your physical health than one that needs ten friends and a pitch, and you can keep it up long after you graduate.

Where to use it
  • Speaking Part 1: Point → Why → Example and stop: roughly thirty seconds per answer.
  • Speaking Part 2: spread the seven steps over the cue-card prompts and keep the Evaluation for the last prompt, the one that starts ‘and explain …’.
  • Speaking Part 3: the full seven steps in roughly a minute, with a short sentence per step.
  • Writing (Sheet 8): you write single sentences, not a speech, but Why and Result are exactly what a Level 3 clause adds: because … (why), , so … or , which … (result).

7 · Common mistakes

MistakeCorrectionRemember
Cadets must to switch off their phones in the lecture hall.Cadets must switch off their phones in the lecture hall.must + bare verb, never to (MLH p. 97).
My roommate doesn't can swim, so he's nervous about the water test.My roommate can't swim, so he's nervous about the water test.can never takes do / does: can't = cannot (MLH p. 97).
It's only a practice game, so you mustn't wear the full kit.It's only a practice game, so you don't have to wear the full kit.not necessary → don't have to; mustn't means it is forbidden (MLH p. 102).
He have to be at the stadium by seven.He has to be at the stadium by seven.he / she / it → has to; questions and negatives with does.
I enjoy to watch basketball more than playing it.I enjoy watching basketball more than playing it.enjoy + -ing, never to (MLH p. 115).
I'm good at play volleyball, but I'm bored with sit on the bench.I'm good at playing volleyball, but I'm bored with sitting on the bench.after a preposition (at, with, of, about) → -ing (MLH pp. 116–117).
Run in the evening helps me sleep.Running in the evening helps me sleep.the subject is a noun or an -ing form, never a bare verb; the verb after it is singular (MLH p. 14).
I want watching the final with you tonight.I want to watch the final with you tonight.want, hope, decide + to + verb (MLH p. 112).
She's a gymnastic, and her brother is a footballer player.She's a gymnast, and her brother is a footballer (or a football player).the person: gymnast, cyclist (never cyclister); footballer or football player, never both endings.
We won the nursing school 2–0 last Saturday.We beat the nursing school 2–0 last Saturday.beat + the other side · win + the game, the race, the cup.
In basketball, you score goals by throwing the ball through the hoop.In basketball, you score points by throwing the ball through the hoop.football, hockey → goals · basketball, tennis, volleyball → points (TB 2a).
More than fifty competitions turned up for the chess tournament.More than fifty competitors turned up for the chess tournament.competitor = a person · competition = the event.

Crazy competitions!

There are lots of competitions in the USA and some of them are a bit crazy!

The Idiotarod

The Idiotarod is an annual race in twenty different US cities. Each team must have five people and a shopping cart. One person usually rides in the cart and four people pull it. Teams can decorate the shopping cart but they can't change the wheels. All the teams have to start and finish at the same place but they don't have to run on the same roads. The members of each team must cross the finish line together and they mustn't finish without the cart!

The Mud Bowl Championship

Mud Bowl football is similar to normal American football, so players can pick up the ball and run with it. There are also two teams, but the match is shorter. The winner is the team with the most goals at the end of sixty minutes. The really big difference is that the players have to play in a field with half a metre of mud!

Crazy competitions!

There are lots of competitions in the USA and some of them are a bit crazy!Q1

AThe Idiotarod

The Idiotarod is an annual race in twenty different US cities.Q2 Each team must have five people and a shopping cart.Q3,Q7,Q12 One person usually rides in the cart and four people pull it.Q3,Q7 Teams can decorate the shopping cart but they can't change the wheels.Q4 All the teams have to start and finish at the same place but they don't have to run on the same roads.Q5,Q6 The members of each team must cross the finish line together and they mustn't finish without the cart!Q6

BThe Mud Bowl Championship

Mud Bowl football is similar to normal American football, so players can pick up the ball and run with it.Q8,Q9,Q11 There are also two teams, but the match is shorter.Q9,Q11,Q12 The winner is the team with the most goals at the end of sixty minutes.Q11 The really big difference is that the players have to play in a field with half a metre of mud!Q10,Q11

Reading A
1There are lots of competitions in the USA and some of them are a bit crazy! What does this first line show about the writer?
1There are lots of competitions in the USA and some of them are a bit crazy! What does this first line show about the writer?
A bit crazy is a friendly way of saying ‘unusual and silly’, and the exclamation mark shows the writer is enjoying the idea. Nothing in the article warns, complains or sneers, and some of them means only some of the competitions, not every one.Clue: a bit softens crazy, and the line ends with !
In the text: There are lots of competitions in the USA and some of them are a bit crazy!
2Put the first sentence of A together with the rules of A. Where and how often does the Idiotarod happen?
2Put the first sentence of A together with the rules of A. Where and how often does the Idiotarod happen?
Each city has its own race once a year, so there are about twenty Idiotarods, not one long race across the country. That also fits the rule that teams start and finish at the same place. The text says nothing about how many years the race has existed, and annual is not monthly.Clue: annual = once a year; in twenty different US cities = in each of those cities.
In the text: The Idiotarod is an annual race in twenty different US cities.
3The writer says that one person usually rides in the cart. What does usually tell us?
3The writer says that one person usually rides in the cart. What does usually tell us?
The writer switches from ‘Each team must have five people’ to ‘usually’, so riding in the cart is a habit, not an obligation. The numbers add up as well: one rider plus four pullers makes the five people the rule asks for, so the rider belongs to the team. Weight, swapping riders and punishments are never mentioned.Clue: Compare must (a rule) in the sentence before with usually (what normally happens).
In the text: Each team must have five people and a shopping cart. One person usually rides in the cart and four people pull it.
4Six teams are getting their carts ready for the Idiotarod. Which team is breaking a rule?
4Six teams are getting their carts ready for the Idiotarod. Which team is breaking a rule?
Paint, wings, flags, cushions and a giant foot (like the one in the photo) are all decoration, and decoration is allowed (can). New wheels are the one change the rule forbids (can't), which keeps every team on the same kind of wheels.Clue: Teams can decorate the shopping cart but they can't change the wheels.
In the text: Teams can decorate the shopping cart but they can't change the wheels.
5… but they don't have to run on the same roads. What does this mean?
5… but they don't have to run on the same roads. What does this mean?
Teams may take the same roads or different ones: the choice is theirs. ‘Must not use the same roads’ turns don't have to into mustn't, the classic mix-up (Sheet 4, section 1). The start and finish are fixed, too: ‘All the teams have to start and finish at the same place.’Clue: don't have to = not necessary but allowed; mustn't = not allowed.
In the text: All the teams have to start and finish at the same place but they don't have to run on the same roads.
6Which of these finishes would the judges accept?
6Which of these finishes would the judges accept?
Only the finish where all five cross side by side, pulling the cart, keeps all three: the whole team arrives at the same moment, the cart comes too, and the line is where they began. A late fifth member, a runner who goes ahead, an empty-handed sprint, a different finish point or a half-team each breaks one of them.Clue: Three rules: start and finish at the same place · cross the finish line together · mustn't finish without the cart.
In the text: All the teams have to start and finish at the same place but they don't have to run on the same roads. The members of each team must cross the finish line together and they mustn't finish without the cart!
7The name Idiotarod is a joke on the Iditarod, a long race across Alaska in which a team of dogs pulls a sled and its driver. Which part of the Idiotarod copies that race?
7The name Idiotarod is a joke on the Iditarod, a long race across Alaska in which a team of dogs pulls a sled and its driver. Which part of the Idiotarod copies that race?
In Alaska, dogs pull the driver on a sled; in the Idiotarod, four team members pull the fifth in a shopping cart. That picture is the joke, and the word idiot inside the name adds to it (TB). Twenty cities, decorations and the choice of roads have nothing to do with sled-dog racing, and the article mentions neither medals nor snow.Clue: One person usually rides in the cart and four people pull it.
In the text: Each team must have five people and a shopping cart. One person usually rides in the cart and four people pull it.
8In the first sentence of B, why does the writer put so between the comparison with American football and the rule about the ball?
8In the first sentence of B, why does the writer put so between the comparison with American football and the rule about the ball?
Normal American football lets players pick up the ball and run, and the Mud Bowl is similar, so the same rule applies. A contrast would need but (it comes in the next sentence: ‘but the match is shorter’). Can means allowed, not obligatory, and the length of the match and the mud come later.Clue: so introduces a result: the first half of the sentence is the reason.
In the text: Mud Bowl football is similar to normal American football, so players can pick up the ball and run with it.
9There are also two teams, but the match is shorter. Shorter than what?
9There are also two teams, but the match is shorter. Shorter than what?
Paragraph B compares the Mud Bowl with ‘normal American football’ from start to finish: similar to, also two teams, but … shorter, the really big difference. A match lasts sixty minutes, so it cannot be shorter than sixty minutes, and the Idiotarod is never compared with it.Clue: A comparative such as shorter looks back to something already named: here, in the first sentence of B.
In the text: Mud Bowl football is similar to normal American football, so players can pick up the ball and run with it. There are also two teams, but the match is shorter.
10According to the writer, what really makes the Mud Bowl different?
10According to the writer, what really makes the Mud Bowl different?
The writer saves the craziest rule for the last sentence and signals it clearly: ‘the players have to play in a field with half a metre of mud!’ That is deep enough to reach most players' knees. Picking up the ball is the same as in normal American football, the match is shorter, not longer, and five people with a cart belong to the Idiotarod.Clue: The really big difference is that …
In the text: The really big difference is that the players have to play in a field with half a metre of mud!
11Which of these does the article not tell us about the Mud Bowl?
11Which of these does the article not tell us about the Mud Bowl?
Paragraph B gives the length (sixty minutes), the number of teams (two), the winner (the team with the most goals), the mud (half a metre) and the ball rule (pick it up and run). The Idiotarod is called annual, but the Mud Bowl paragraph never says how often it is held (SB Ex 3.3).Clue: Check each option against paragraph B: five are there, one is missing.
In the text: Mud Bowl football is similar to normal American football, so players can pick up the ball and run with it. There are also two teams, but the match is shorter. The winner is the team with the most goals at the end of sixty minutes. The really big difference is that the players have to play in a field with half a metre of mud!
12Which of these is true of both competitions?
12Which of these is true of both competitions?
also links B back to the teams in A, so teams are the one thing the two competitions share (SB Ex 3.5). The time limit and the borrowed rules belong to the Mud Bowl; the cart, the shared start and finish and annual belong to the Idiotarod.Clue: A: Each team must have five people; B: There are also two teams.
In the text: Each team must have five people and a shopping cart. There are also two teams, but the match is shorter.

3 · Extra practice · PET Reading Part 3 · The first Ironman: a race that started with an argument

Questions 11–15. Read the article about the first Ironman. Choose the right answer, A–F.

Passage | Questions

The first Ironman: a race that started with an argument

Today, thousands of athletes dream of finishing an Ironman: a 3.86-kilometre swim, a 180-kilometre bike ride and a full marathon, one straight after the other. But the first Ironman was not planned by a sports company. It grew out of a friendly argument at a party.Q11

In 1977, runners and swimmers in Hawaii were at the prize-giving for a relay race around the island of Oahu when a question came up: who were fitter, runners or swimmers? John Collins, an officer in the US Navy, had a third answer. He had read in a magazine that tests on a famous Belgian cyclist showed that his body could use more oxygen than any other athlete's ever measured, so perhaps cyclists were the fittest of all.Q12 To settle the argument, he and his wife, Judy, suggested joining three of the island's toughest races into one: a 2.4-mile swim, a 112-mile bike race and a marathon.Q15 Whoever finished first, Collins said, would be called the ‘Iron Man’.

The race took place on 18 February 1978. Fifteen men started in the sea at Waikiki.Q13,Q15 Each athlete had to bring his own support crew to give him food and water along the way.Q13 Before the start, every competitor received three sheets of paper with the rules.Q13 On the last page, Collins had written by hand: ‘Swim 2.4 miles! Bike 112 miles! Run 26.2 miles! Brag for the rest of your life!’

After the bike ride, the leader was John Dunbar, a Navy SEAL, who started the marathon with a thirteen-minute lead. But his crew ran out of water, and they gave him beer instead.Q14 Gordon Haller, a 27-year-old, caught him on the run and crossed the finish line after 11 hours and 46 minutes; Dunbar came second.Q14 Collins himself finished in just over seventeen hours.Q14

Twelve of the fifteen starters reached the finish, and none of them could have guessed what would happen next.Q15 After a sports magazine wrote about the second race in 1979, 108 athletes entered the next one, and in 1981 the race moved to the Big Island of Hawaii. Today there are Ironman races all over the world, but the question that started it all has never really been answered.Q15

PET 3

It grew out of a friendly argument …
In the text: But the first Ironman was not planned by a sports company. It grew out of a friendly argument at a party.

The text does not say he cycled himself, and the relay race was for runners and swimmers: nobody says a cyclist won it.Clue: Paragraph 2: He had read in a magazine that tests on a famous Belgian cyclist …

There were no helpers from the organisers, so every athlete brought his own crew for food and water. Dunbar was ahead at the start of the run, but Haller caught him and won. Nobody was disqualified.Clue: Paragraph 4: … started the marathon with a thirteen-minute lead … Dunbar came second.

My first half marathon

5 · After reading · Talk about it

Talk about each question with a partner. Then open the model answer.

1 · Why do people enjoy watching or joining crazy competitions like the Idiotarod?

Model answer

PointI think the big attraction is that nobody takes them seriously, so the usual pressure of sport simply disappears. WhyYou can't really be bad at pushing a shopping cart in fancy dress, so people who would never enter a normal race are happy to give it a go. HowThe silly rules turn the event into a street party, where the crowd cheers the funniest team as loudly as the fastest one. ExampleMy cousin's university in Đà Nẵng holds a slow bicycle race every spring: the winner is the last rider to reach the line without putting a foot on the ground. ResultWhen he took me along, hundreds of students were screaming for riders who were hardly moving, and the champion needed almost four minutes to cover thirty metres. LimitationNot everyone loves these events, though; some people find them childish, and the crowds can leave the streets in a mess. EvaluationStill, anything that gets people moving and laughing together is worth a bit of noise, in my view.

2 · Is it a good idea to change the rules of a real sport to make it funny, as the Mud Bowl does?

Model answer

PointI'd say yes, as long as everyone knows it's a bit of fun and not the real game. WhyOne crazy rule, like playing in deep mud, makes skill matter less, so beginners can play alongside good players without feeling useless. HowThe basic rules stay the same, so nobody has to learn a new game, but the twist makes every match hard to predict. ExampleAt a summer camp near Huế a few years ago, the leaders organised a football match with a giant inflatable ball that was almost as tall as the players. ResultThe ball bounced off people in every direction, the strongest boys kept getting knocked over, and a twelve-year-old girl who had never played football scored the winning goal. LimitationThe danger is that a funny version can be a less safe one: mud hides stones, and a huge ball can knock people off their feet, so someone has to check the ground and keep the games short. EvaluationSo I'm all for silly versions of real sports, but safety is the one rule I'd never change.

3 · Would you rather compete in a team or on your own? Why?

Model answer

PointGiven the choice, I'd rather compete in a team than on my own. WhyI simply try harder when other people are counting on me: when I run alone and it starts to hurt, I slow down, but I hate letting teammates down. HowIn a team everyone has a job, and you can see exactly how your part helps the group. ExampleIn the team cross-country race at the end of basic training, each platoon's time was the time of its last runner, so all ten of us had to stay together. ResultOn the final hill our slowest runner started to fade, so two of us ran either side of him and talked him all the way up, and we finished third out of twelve platoons. LimitationThe downside is that you can't control everything: one person's bad day can cost the whole team, however hard you train. EvaluationEven so, that race taught me more about looking after people than any race I've run alone, and that's a lesson every doctor needs.

4 · Should a medical academy hold sports competitions for its cadets?

Model answer

PointYes, I think it definitely should, and more than once a year. WhyMost of us will work long night shifts one day, and a fit body copes far better with little sleep and hours on your feet; a competition gives people a real reason to get fit now. HowA few events each term, with separate levels for beginners and strong athletes, would give everyone something realistic to aim for. ExampleWhen the academy held a three-on-three basketball tournament last month, Hiếu, the quietest cadet in our room, signed up because our team was one player short. ResultHe practised free throws on the outdoor court every evening for three weeks, and in our last game he scored the basket that took us into the semi-final. LimitationThe risk is that some cadets push too hard and get injured just before exams or a field exercise. EvaluationWith sensible rules and a medical team at every event, though, the benefits are well worth that risk.

For or against competitive sports in schools? · SB p. 25 Ex 6

  1. Winning and losing teaches students about life.

  8. All children are different and some aren't good at sport.
  9. Competitive sports are fun.
Key · For (F) or against (A)? Who says which?

F 1, 3, 5, 6, 9 · A 2, 4, 7, 8

Speaker 1 → 1, 3, 5, 6 · Speaker 2 → 2, 4, 8 · Speaker 3 → 7, 9 (SB Ex 7)

Listening A
1Speaker 1 gives several reasons for competitive sport in schools. Which reason is missing from what Speaker 1 says?
1Speaker 1 gives several reasons for competitive sport in schools. Which reason is missing from what Speaker 1 says?
Speaker 1 never mentions future champions or top athletes. Every other option is in the recording, some in other words: ‘it teaches you about life’, ‘good for their physical health’, ‘they work harder and get more exercise’, ‘you learn to work well in teams’.Clue: Tick off the reasons as you hear them: life, physical health, working harder, more exercise, teams.
In the text: Learning to win and lose is important in a child's education because it teaches you about life. They're also good for their physical health, because when children try to win, they work harder and get more exercise. The other good thing about competitive sports is that you learn to work well in teams when you play in matches. Competitions are a great lesson in teamwork.
2Which of these would Speaker 1 most probably agree with?
2Which of these would Speaker 1 most probably agree with?
For Speaker 1, winning and losing are the lesson, so a sports day without results would take it away. Finland and the parents belong to Speakers 2 and 3, and Speaker 1 says teamwork is learned when you ‘play in matches’.Clue: Learning to win and lose is important … + a great lesson in teamwork
In the text: Learning to win and lose is important in a child's education because it teaches you about life. So I think competitive sports in schools are good for teaching children. The other good thing about competitive sports is that you learn to work well in teams when you play in matches. Competitions are a great lesson in teamwork.
3That's really bad for the child. What does That refer to?
3That's really bad for the child. What does That refer to?
The sentence before is ‘when school sports are competitive, they always lose.’ Speaker 2's worry is the child who loses every time. Not liking sport comes next, as a separate point, and the shouting parents are Speaker 3's.Clue: That refers to an idea in the previous sentence.
In the text: Some children aren't good at sport, so when school sports are competitive, they always lose. That's really bad for the child.
4Why does Speaker 2 talk about schools in Finland?
4Why does Speaker 2 talk about schools in Finland?
Finland is Speaker 2's proof that schools can do well without competition, so schools ‘in my country’ could change too. Finnish schools still have sport, just not competitive sport, and the example shows the opposite of ‘competition leads to good results’.Clue: They get good results but they aren't competitive …
In the text: I think schools in my country should be more like the schools in Finland. They get good results but they aren't competitive and they don't have competitive sports either.
5… and they don't have competitive sports either. What does either add?
5… and they don't have competitive sports either. What does either add?
The first negative is general: ‘they aren't competitive’. either adds a second one: not in sport, too. There is no choice between two things here, and nothing is said about dates, parents or doubt.Clue: not … either = also not, after another negative.
In the text: They get good results but they aren't competitive and they don't have competitive sports either.
6… that's OK as long as they do their best. Which sentence means the same?
6… that's OK as long as they do their best. Which sentence means the same?
Speaker 2 puts one condition on ‘that's OK’: real effort. As long as is about a condition here, not a length of time, and Speaker 2 never promises that trying hard leads to winning or suggests changing sport.Clue: as long as = only if, on condition that (Sheet 3 · Group 4).
In the text: So when a child can't do a sport very well, that's OK as long as they do their best and try hard at everything they do.
7Who is Speaker 3 most probably?
7Who is Speaker 3 most probably?
my school + the children sounds like an adult who works there: a pupil would say ‘we love it’. Speaker 3 also talks about ‘some of the mothers and fathers’ as other people, not as one of them. Finland is Speaker 2's example, and the Olympic Games are only a joke.Clue: We have a sports day at my school and the children love it.
In the text: We have a sports day at my school and the children love it. Some parents hate losing and they get very competitive. When there's a race or a match, some of them shout at their kids.
8According to Speaker 3, where is the real problem?
8According to Speaker 3, where is the real problem?
Speaker 3 first says what is not the problem (competitive sport) and then names the real one: parents who ‘hate losing’, ‘get very competitive’ and ‘shout at their kids’. The children love the day, and teachers are never mentioned.Clue: I don't think there's a problem with … ; the problem is with …
In the text: So, overall, I don't think there's a problem with having competitive sports in school; the problem is with some of the mothers and fathers. Some parents hate losing and they get very competitive. When there's a race or a match, some of them shout at their kids.
9They think it's the Olympic Games or something! What is Speaker 3 doing?
9They think it's the Olympic Games or something! What is Speaker 3 doing?
A school race is nothing like the Olympic Games; the comparison shows how silly the shouting parents look. It is criticism said with a smile, not praise and not a real comparison.Clue: or something + ! = an exaggeration that makes a point.
In the text: Some parents hate losing and they get very competitive. When there's a race or a match, some of them shout at their kids. They think it's the Olympic Games or something!
10What do Speakers 1 and 3 agree about?
10What do Speakers 1 and 3 agree about?
Speaker 1 is for competitive sport and Speaker 3 sees no problem with it, so both accept it in schools (SB Ex 5: Speaker 1 = b, Speaker 3 = c). The parents are only Speaker 3's point, weak children and Finland only Speaker 2's, teamwork only Speaker 1's.Clue: Speaker 1: competitive sports in schools are good … · Speaker 3: I don't think there's a problem with having competitive sports in school
In the text: So I think competitive sports in schools are good for teaching children. So, overall, I don't think there's a problem with having competitive sports in school; the problem is with some of the mothers and fathers.

5 · Extra practice · PET Listening Part 4 · A doctor who does triathlons

Questions 20–25. Listen to an interview with Dr Thảo Lê, a young doctor who does triathlons. Choose the best answer.

Audio + transcript | Questions
Played 0×

Press Show answers to open the transcript.

Transcript

PresenterGood evening, and welcome to Active Lives. My guest tonight is Dr Thảo Lê, a junior doctor in the emergency department of a big city hospital, who spends her free time doing triathlons. Thảo, how did it all begin?

ThảoWith an injury, actually. I used to run, and in my second year at medical school I hurt my knee quite badly. The physiotherapist told me to stop running for three months and to swim and cycle instead.Q20 By the time my knee was better, I was enjoying the swimming and cycling more than the running!

PresenterAnd then you put all three together.

ThảoYes. A friend from my course dared me to enter a sprint triathlon: seven hundred and fifty metres of swimming, twenty kilometres on the bike and a five-kilometre run. I said yes before I'd really thought about it.

PresenterHow did your first race go?

ThảoThe bike and the run were fine. The swim was the hard part. In the pool you have your own lane, but in open water you've got a hundred people all around you, kicking and splashing.Q21 I swallowed half the lake! I had to stop and hold on to a safety boat for a minute before I could go on.Q21

PresenterYou work long shifts. When do you find time to train?

ThảoI build it into my day. I cycle to the hospital and back, which is twenty-five minutes each way, and I swim at the hospital pool before my shift starts. I never train hard after a night shift, though. Sleep comes first.Q22

PresenterDo you race to win?

ThảoNot really. I'm usually somewhere in the middle. What I care about is beating my own time from the last race. If I'm one minute faster, I'm delighted, whatever place I finish.Q23

PresenterHas triathlon changed the way you work as a doctor?

ThảoI think so. I know now how hard it is to change your habits, so I don't just tell patients to do more exercise. I suggest one small step, like walking to the market instead of taking the motorbike, and we build from there.Q24

PresenterAnd what's next for you? A full Ironman?

ThảoMaybe one day, but not yet: that's a whole year of training. Next year I want to do a relay triathlon with two colleagues from the department. One swims, one cycles and one runs, so they can try it without doing all three.Q25

PresenterDr Thảo Lê, thank you, and good luck.

Sheet 7 / 11 · Speaking · Part 1 interview · Part 2 long turn (HP1 card A, HP4 card B) · Part 3 discussion

Speaking

In the model answers:
  • Point Why … (coloured tags) = the steps of the answer frame: Point, Why, How, Example, Result, Limitation, Evaluation
  • frame language = phrases that give an opinion, a reason, an example, a contrast or a conclusion
  • unit vocabulary = words from the four Sheet 3 groups of this lesson
What each step does · Part 1: Point, Why, Example · Parts 2 and 3: all sevenPointsay your answerWhygive the reasonHowshow how it worksExampleone real caseResultwhat came of itLimitationthe weak pointEvaluationyour view at the end

Part 1 · Interview: sport, watching sport, winning and losing (10 questions, 30 seconds each)

0:30Answer = Point → Why → Example
Record practice — Part 1
Warm-up · SB p. 25, Ex 13

Ask your partner which sports and free-time activities they like, then finish the five sentences about the two of you.

A: What sports do you love watching? B: Tennis. What about you?

Then use the frames below for the ten interview questions.

Topic 1Sport and exerciseLet's talk about sport and exercise.

Topic 2Watching sportLet's talk about watching sport.

Record practice — Part 2

Choose card A or B. Note key words for 1 minute. Then speak for 2 minutes and answer every prompt.

Card AYour favourite sportHP1 bank, topic 4
