LimitationAdmittedly, it's hard to fit in here: on a busy night you … EvaluationEven so, I enjoy it more than … It's …, it's … and it makes me … After a day of …, chasing … clears my head better than …

Model answer · Cue card A · about 260 words (2 minutes)

PointMy favourite sport is badminton, a racket game where you hit a shuttlecock, a little cork with sixteen feathers, over a high net. WhyI've picked it because it's the one sport I've never given up. I got into it at about eight: on summer evenings, my mum and the neighbours tied a rope between two lamp posts in our alley and played till dark, and one night she handed me her racket: ‘Your turn.’ HowIt's simple to play but hard to master: you can't let the shuttle land on your side, you can't touch the net, and every serve has to go diagonally across the court, so the whole game is about sending the shuttle where your opponent isn't. ExampleI play on the academy courts after evening study. The game I remember best was in last month's cadets' tournament: I was really worried about facing a fourth-year a head taller than me, and in the third game he needed one more point. But I kept the shuttle low and won the next five. ResultI won the match, and my opponent invited me to train with his group on Thursday nights. I haven't missed one since. LimitationAdmittedly, it's hard to fit in here: on a busy night you wait half an hour for a court. EvaluationEven so, I enjoy it more than anything else I play. It's fast, it's cheap and it makes me think ahead. After a day of lectures, chasing a shuttle for forty minutes clears my head better than a nap.

Card A · 3 prompts + last line · 7 steps
Look again
  • … a racket game where you hit a shuttlecock … — What the sport is: the name first, then a plain picture of the game for someone who has never played it
  • one night she handed me her racket: ‘Your turn.’ — prompt 2 (how you got interested) sits inside the Why: one small scene from childhood says more than ‘I became interested when I was young’
  • you can't let the shuttle land on your side, you can't touch the net, and every serve has to go diagonally across the court — the How explains how the game works, with verbs for rules (Sheet 4, section 1): can't = not allowed, have to = obligatory
  • I was really worried about facing a fourth-year … — prompt 3 (have you played it?): yes, and one match told shot by shot; an -ing form after a preposition (worried about facing, Sheet 4, section 2) and Group 1 words (a tournament, a point, an opponent)
  • … chasing a shuttle for forty minutes clears my head … — explain why you enjoy it: three short reasons, then the -ing form as the subject with a singular verb (chasing … clears), so the Evaluation adds something the Point did not say

Card BA game that is popular in your countryHP4 bank, topic 6

PointThe game I'm going to talk about is …, which is easily the most popular game in … WhyI've chosen it because almost everyone here has …, whether they …, … or just … HowTwo teams of … try to …, and only the … can use his hands, inside … Most people, though, play … on …, and just about everyone plays: …, …, even … ExampleBut what really shows how much people love it is … In December 2019, Vietnam's … team beat … in the SEA Games final in … and won the men's football gold for the first time in … ResultThat night my whole family was …, and after the final whistle the streets filled with … The next weekend, my little brother's friends were all pretending to be … LimitationAdmittedly, the national team still hasn't made it to …, and celebrating … isn't exactly … EvaluationStill, I can see why it's so … Playing it costs …, you can find a game …, and when the national team wins, …

Model answer · Cue card B · about 240 words (2 minutes)

PointThe game I'm going to talk about is football, which is easily the most popular game in Vietnam. WhyI've chosen it because almost everyone here has a football story, whether they play, watch or just join the party in the street afterwards. HowTwo teams of eleven try to score goals, and only the goalkeeper can use his hands, inside his own box. Most people, though, play five-a-side on small artificial pitches rented by the hour, and just about everyone plays: kids after school, office workers after work, even grandfathers on Sunday mornings. ExampleBut what really shows how much people love it is the national team. In December 2019, Vietnam's under-22 team beat Indonesia three nil in the SEA Games final in Manila and won the men's football gold for the first time in sixty years. ResultThat night my whole family was shouting at the TV, and after the final whistle the streets filled with red flags and honking motorbikes until after midnight. The next weekend, my little brother's friends were all pretending to be Đoàn Văn Hậu, the defender who scored two of the goals. LimitationAdmittedly, the national team still hasn't made it to a World Cup, and celebrating on a motorbike at midnight isn't exactly safe. EvaluationStill, I can see why it's so popular. Playing it costs next to nothing, you can find a game anywhere, and when the national team wins, the whole country feels like it's won too.

Card B · 3 prompts + last line · 7 steps
Look again
  • … only the goalkeeper can use his hands … — How it is played: two rules are enough (a number, a verb for rules), then how people really play it
  • … kids after school, office workers after work, even grandfathers on Sunday mornings — Who plays it: three groups from young to old, clearer than ‘many people’
  • In December 2019, Vietnam's under-22 team beat Indonesia three nil in the SEA Games final in Manila … — one checked fact (a month, an opponent, a score) makes the talk sound informed; beat + the team you defeat, win + the match, the title or the trophy (never won Indonesia)
  • That night my whole family was shouting at the TV … — the Result belongs to that one final: what you saw and heard that night and the weekend after
  • Playing it costs next to nothing … — explain why it is popular: the -ing form as the subject (singular verb costs), then two more reasons in new words, not the Point again

Choose card A or B. Plan one line per step, then speak for 2 minutes.

1:00Frame: Point Why How Example Result Limitation Evaluation
Record practice — Part 3

Four topics, ten questions. Give each answer about a minute and use the seven steps.

Topic 1Competitive sport for children

1 · At what age should children start taking part in competitions?

PointI'd say around …, once they can … WhyYounger kids mostly want to …, and if you add … too early, many of them … HowBefore that age, games can have rules but no winners: everyone …, nobody …, and the coach … ExampleMy little cousin, for example, was entered in … at … and came last … ResultShe cried all the way home and wouldn't … for … LimitationThen again, some children love competing from the start, and holding them back can … EvaluationSo parents don't have to follow … They just need to watch …, not …

HowBefore that age, games can have rules but no winners: everyone plays, nobody counts the goals, and the coach praises effort. ExampleMy little cousin, for example, was entered in a swimming race at five and came last by half a length, in front of a pool full of parents. ResultShe cried all the way home and wouldn't get back in the water for almost a year. LimitationThen again, some children love competing from the start, and holding them back can put them off just as much. EvaluationSo parents don't have to follow a fixed age. They just need to watch the child, not the scoreboard.

2 · Do parents put too much pressure on children who play sport?

PointIn my view, some do, and it's often the ones who … WhyThey see their child's match as …, so a normal mistake … HowYou can spot them at any junior game: they coach louder than … and argue with … ExampleAt my brother's … game last spring, for instance, one father kept shouting at … until … ResultThe coach took the boy off, and the club made a new rule: parents have to … LimitationAdmittedly, a lot of kids wouldn't … without … EvaluationOn balance, a little push helps, but when every game feels like …, kids …

Model answer

PointIn my view, some do, and it's often the ones who never made it themselves. WhyThey see their child's match as a second chance, so a normal mistake feels like a disaster. HowYou can spot them at any junior game: they coach louder than the coach and argue with the referee over every decision. ExampleAt my brother's under-11 basketball game last spring, for instance, one father kept shouting at his son until the boy missed an easy pass and burst into tears. ResultThe coach took the boy off, and the club made a new rule: parents have to sit in the stands and keep quiet. LimitationAdmittedly, a lot of kids wouldn't train at all without a parent pushing them a bit. EvaluationOn balance, a little push helps, but when every game feels like an exam, kids quit.

3 · Should every child get a medal just for taking part?

PointPersonally, I don't think so, at least not after the age of … WhyKids aren't stupid. If everybody gets the same …, they soon work out … HowIt's better to reward something any child can achieve, like … or … ExampleMy sister's primary school, for example, gave … to all … children at last year's sports day, even … ResultShe came home, dropped hers in … and said, ‘…’ She hasn't … LimitationThen again, for very young children a medal is …, and it does … EvaluationSo I'd keep medals for … and, after that, give prizes that …

Model answer

PointPersonally, I don't think so, at least not after the age of about seven. WhyKids aren't stupid. If everybody gets the same medal, they soon work out that it doesn't mean much. HowIt's better to reward something any child can achieve, like being the most improved player or showing the best teamwork. ExampleMy sister's primary school, for example, gave gold medals to all ninety children at last year's sports day, even the ones who'd sat out most of the races. ResultShe came home, dropped hers in a toy box and said, ‘Everyone got one.’ She hasn't looked at it since. LimitationThen again, for very young children a medal is a nice memory of a fun day, and it does no harm. EvaluationSo I'd keep medals for the little ones and, after that, give prizes that children actually have to earn.

Topic 2Rules, referees and fair play

4 · Has video technology made sport fairer?

PointMostly yes, I'd say, especially in …, where one wrong call can … WhyA referee sees each moment once, at …, while the cameras … HowWith VAR, officials watching … can tell the referee …, and he can … ExampleTake the 2018 World Cup, the first to use … In France's opening game against …, the referee waved play on when …, but after a VAR review he … ResultGriezmann scored, France won …, and it went down as the first World Cup penalty … LimitationThen again, reviews can take …, and fans in the stadium often … EvaluationWeighing it all up, I'd rather wait … for the right call than …

Model answer

PointMostly yes, I'd say, especially in football, where one wrong call can decide a tournament. WhyA referee sees each moment once, at full speed, while the cameras can replay it from every angle. HowWith VAR, officials watching replays can tell the referee he's missed something, and he can check a screen beside the pitch. ExampleTake the 2018 World Cup, the first to use it. In France's opening game against Australia, the referee waved play on when Antoine Griezmann went down in the box, but after a VAR review he gave a penalty. ResultGriezmann scored, France won two-one, and it went down as the first World Cup penalty given with VAR's help. LimitationThen again, reviews can take ages, and fans in the stadium often have no idea what's happening. EvaluationWeighing it all up, I'd rather wait two minutes for the right call than lose a match to a mistake.

5 · Why do some players break the rules even when they know they might get caught?

PointTo my mind, it's because the reward looks … and the risk looks … WhyWhen the prize is …, … or …, many people convince themselves … HowIt usually starts small, too: one shortcut, then …, until breaking the rules … ExampleLance Armstrong is the obvious … He won the Tour de France … times in a row, from … to …, and the whole time he was … ResultIn 2012 he was stripped of … and banned …, and in January 2013 he finally … LimitationAdmittedly, he wasn't the only cyclist … back then, and some blame … EvaluationEven so, people cheat when they think …, so strict testing does more to … than any speech about …

Model answer

PointTo my mind, it's because the reward looks huge and the risk looks small. WhyWhen the prize is a trophy, fame or a fortune, many people convince themselves they'll never get caught. HowIt usually starts small, too: one shortcut, then another, until breaking the rules feels normal. ExampleLance Armstrong is the obvious case. He won the Tour de France seven times in a row, from 1999 to 2005, and the whole time he was taking banned drugs. ResultIn 2012 he was stripped of all seven titles and banned for life, and in January 2013 he finally admitted it in a TV interview. LimitationAdmittedly, he wasn't the only cyclist doping back then, and some blame the whole sport, not one man. EvaluationEven so, people cheat when they think nobody is checking, so strict testing does more to keep sport clean than any speech about fair play.

Instead, he … LimitationAdmittedly, it was a small race with …, and it's much harder to be that generous in … EvaluationStill, the video of that moment went viral in …, and I'd show it to …

Model answer

HowCoaches can show those moments to young players and praise honesty as loudly as a goal. ExampleA good example of this is a cross-country race in Spain in December 2012. The leader, the Kenyan runner Abel Mutai, slowed right down near the end because he thought he'd already finished. ResultIván Fernández Anaya, the Spanish runner behind him, could have gone past and won. Instead, he pointed the way and let Mutai cross the line first. LimitationAdmittedly, it was a small race with little at stake, and it's much harder to be that generous in an Olympic final. EvaluationStill, the video of that moment went viral in 2013, and I'd show it to every junior team in the country.

ExampleTake the army swimmer Nguyễn Thị Ánh Viên, who won eight gold medals at the 2015 SEA Games in Singapore and broke a Games record in every one of those races. EvaluationThat's why I believe young people should choose their heroes carefully, and for a cadet, a champion in uniform who trained at dawn for years is hard to beat.

8 · Should sports stars be punished for bad behaviour away from their sport?

PointYes, if you ask me, when what they did hurts … or … WhyTheir fame comes from the sport, so it's fair that … HowSports federations can … Sponsors can …, and that often … ExampleA case in point is the American swimmer … at … He said …, but really … ResultWithin weeks, … of his main sponsors had dropped him, and he was suspended from competing for … LimitationAdmittedly, nobody's perfect, and the media can turn … into … EvaluationOverall, though, if a famous athlete wants to be paid like a role model, he has to …

Model answer

PointYes, if you ask me, when what they did hurts other people or the sport's good name. WhyTheir fame comes from the sport, so it's fair that the sport can take some of it back. HowSports federations can suspend them. Sponsors can simply walk away, and that often hurts more. ExampleA case in point is the American swimmer Ryan Lochte at the 2016 Rio Olympics. LimitationAdmittedly, nobody's perfect, and the media can turn a small mistake into a scandal overnight. PointTo be honest, they have to forget about free time and use the small gaps. WhyAfter a twenty-four-hour duty, nobody has energy for the gym, yet the WHO still recommends at least a hundred and fifty minutes of moderate exercise a week. HowThat's only about twenty minutes a day, and you can get exercise in pieces: the stairs instead of the lift, a fast walk to the canteen. ExampleOn my hospital placement last summer, for example, the head of surgery, nearly sixty, never once took the lift to his seventh-floor ward. ResultA month later I was the one gasping behind him, and he said the stairs were his only gym. LimitationAdmittedly, after a night shift even the stairs feel like a mountain. Sleep has to come first. EvaluationAll in all, the free hour never comes in this job, so the minutes you do have are the ones that count.

Model answer

PointPersonally, I think they should, even if it's only ten minutes a shift. WhyTired, stiff staff make mistakes. Moving for a few minutes wakes the brain up better than coffee. HowIt doesn't have to be fancy: just a set time when everyone stands up and does the same simple routine. ExampleAt the military hospital where my aunt is a nurse, for example, the surgical ward started a five-minute stretch at ten every morning last year, led by the head nurse. ResultShe says fewer of the staff complain of back pain now, and some patients even join in from their beds. LimitationThen again, nobody in an emergency department can promise a calm ten minutes, so the timing has to be flexible. EvaluationOn balance, if every Vietnamese school can stop for a few minutes of exercise in the middle of the morning, a hospital full of health experts certainly can.

Practise 3

Choose 3 questions from three topics. Plan one line per step, then give each answer in about a minute.

Sheet 8 / 11 · Writing · upgrading a sentence · Levels 1–3, Level 4 optional

Writing: upgrade a sentence, level by level

1 Correct → effective2 Level 13 Level 24 Level 35 Keep it correct6 Level 4 ★7 Ladders8 Your ladders

Stage 1 A correct sentence, an effective sentence

Theory · correct, then effective
  • Correct: at least one independent clause (a subject + a verb that shows the time) and one complete idea.
  • Effective: clear and precise, joined with the right word, with the right punctuation.
  • Clause: its own subject + verb (the train left the station). Phrase: no subject–verb pair; it adds detail (at the station · after lunch).
  • Independent clause: can stand alone. Dependent clause: starts with because, when, if, although, which, who and cannot stand alone.
  • The four levels of an upgrade (Level 4 is optional):
    1. Level 1 · BasicS + V (+ O): one short clauseStudents use smartphones.
    2. Level 2 · Detail+ words and phrases: who exactly, what kind, where, when, how oftenMost university students use their smartphones for several hours every day.
    3. Level 3 · Clause+ a clause, most often a reason or a result: because, so, whichMost university students use their smartphones for several hours every day, which leaves them less time for reading.
    4. Level 4 · Academicoptional · encouragedan action → a noun · a careful verb (may, tend to, is likely to) · strong word partnersHeavy smartphone use among university students is likely to reduce the time for reading, which may weaken their concentration.

    Colour key subject verb object / complement connector dependent clause relative clause modifying phrase

  • Keep the same main idea at every level.
Stage 1a

Which level is it?

0/10
Each answer is used twice.
1Prices rose.
Nothing but a subject and a verb, and still a complete idea.
2Many families in big cities buy fresh vegetables at local markets every morning.
Details only (who exactly, what kind, where, when) and still one clause.
3The bus service improved because the city bought fifty new electric buses.
Two clauses: the main one, and because the city bought fifty new electric buses for the reason.
4Although online courses are cheaper than classes on campus.
Only the Although part, with no main clause after it. Finish it: …, many students still prefer a real classroom.
5The growing use of private cars may increase air pollution in large cities.
The idea more and more people use cars has become a noun phrase (The growing use of …), and may keeps the claim careful.
6Tourists complained.
Subject + verb: the shortest correct pattern.
7Working from home three days a week.
An -ing phrase with no finite verb. Add one: Working from home three days a week saves travel time.
8My sister lost her job last year, so she started an online clothes shop.
Two clauses joined by , so: the lost job and its result.
9A shortage of affordable housing in big cities is likely to push young families to the suburbs.
A noun phrase as the subject (A shortage of …) and a careful verb (is likely to).
10A young engineer from Đà Nẵng designed a cheap water filter for rural schools.
Words and phrases (what kind of engineer, from where, what kind of filter, for whom) but only one verb.
Stage 1b

Clause or phrase?

0/9
Look at the words in bold.
1When the factory closed, hundreds of workers lost their jobs.
When + subject + verb: a clause, but it cannot stand alone.
2Mai checks her email three times a day at work.
No subject–verb pair: it answers how often?
3The government built a new hospital because the old one was too small.
Subject + verb + object: it could be a sentence on its own.
4Many young people buy their clothes on shopping websites.
on + a place (here, online), no verb: a phrase that answers where?
5Fewer tourists visited the island because the flights were expensive.
because + subject + verb: a dependent clause; here the main clause comes before it.
6After the storm, volunteers cleaned the beach.
After + a noun, no verb: a phrase. After the storm ended would be a clause.
7Most of the students passed the exam, but a few had to take it again.
Subject + verb + object: it can stand alone. , but then joins a second clause.
8Thousands of commuters wait at the central bus station.
A place, no verb: where?
9The new library opens on the first Monday of September.
on + a day: a time phrase.

Stage 2 Level 1 · Basic: one correct clause

Theory · Level 1, the core
  • Find the verb first: it shows the time (works, worked, has changed, will open).
  • Ask who / what + verb? to find the subject; ask verb + what / whom? to find the object.
  • A complement describes the subject (after be, become, seem, feel, look) or the object (after make: made the area very popular).
  • Five basic patterns:S VThe babyS sleptV.S V OOur teacherS checkedV the homeworkO.S V CThe airS becameV cleanerC.S V O OThe companyS gaveV each workerO a laptopO.S V O CThe new parkS madeV the areaO very popularC.
  • The verb agrees with the main subject: The factory employs · The factories employ · The quality of the roads is poor.
  • Three traps. No subject: ✗ Is a serious problem in big cities. ✓ Traffic is a serious problem in big cities. No verb: ✗ The classroom very hot. ✓ The classroom was very hot. be + a base verb: ✗ We are study online at night. ✓ We study online at night.
Stage 2a

Name the part in bold

0/9
1Our English teacher seems very strict.
Who seems strict? Our English teacher.
2The old bridge became a symbol of the city.
became shows the time (past) and links the bridge to what it turned into.
3The hospital gave every nurse a free flu vaccine.
Who received something? Every nurse: the first object.
4Fast food makes many children overweight.
It describes the children after make + object; nothing is done to it.
5My grandparents listen to the news on an old radio.
No verb: it tells you how they listen. This is Level 2 detail.
6The farmers lost their crops, but they did not give up.
but links the second idea to the first: it belongs to neither clause.
7Plastic bags pollute rivers and beaches.
The action, in the present simple: plural, to agree with bags.
8Online shopping saves time.
What does it save? Time.
9The streets of Hà Nội looked very quiet during the holiday.
It describes the streets after looked.
Stage 2b

A correct Level 1 sentence

0/5
1Which is a correct Level 1 sentence?
B has a subject and a finite verb. A has no subject, C no verb, D puts are before a base verb.
2Which is a correct Level 1 sentence?
The main subject is the number (singular), so has. B has no finite verb; D needs the plural cars after of.
3Which is a correct Level 1 sentence?
D: subject + was + a complement. A has two subjects, B no verb, C needs the adjective confusing.
4Which is a correct Level 1 sentence?
Each of + a plural noun takes a singular verb: has. A uses have, C drops of, D needs the plural students.
5Which is a correct Level 1 sentence?
English order is subject + verb + object: A. B and C change the order, D has no finite verb.

Write a Level 1 sentence

Your turn. Write one Level 1 sentence about your daily life, your studies or your town: a subject + a verb (+ an object or a complement), three to seven words.
Two models

1My roommate cooks dinner.

2The morning bus was late.

Stage 3 Level 2 · Detail: add words and phrases

Theory · Level 2, detail
  • Ask the questions, then add the answers: who exactly? what kind? where? when? how often / how much?
  • Adjectives and nouns go before the noun: a part-time job · a city bus · the children's hospital.
  • Details usually go after the verb and its object, in this order: how, where, when. NamS workedV hardhow at a local caféwhere last summerwhen.
  • Swap a vague word for a precise one: a lot → for two hours a day · good → cheap and reliable · do exercise → go jogging.
  • From Level 1 to Level 2:
    1. Level 1 · BasicPeople recycle.
    2. Level 2 · DetailMany families in my neighbourhood recycle plastic bottles at the community centre every weekend.Added:+ Many families in my neighbourhood who exactly?+ plastic bottles what?+ at the community centre where?+ every weekend how often?
  • No new clause yet: a second subject + verb belongs to Level 3. Aim for about 10–18 words.
Stage 3a

Which detail answers the question?

0/6
The tag says which question the detail must answer.
1how often? My father reads the newspaper ….
every morning answers how often. at the kitchen table answers where, last Sunday is one time, not a habit.
2what kind? The … workers went home early.
An adjective goes before the noun: the exhausted workers. exhaustedly is an adverb, and the others cannot stand before a noun.
3where? My cousin works ….
Where? at + a place. The others answer how often, how, with whom and since when.
4when? The new metro line opens ….
When? at + a clock time. on the west side of the city is where, with a short speech is how.
5who exactly? … volunteers planted trees along the river.
Only Forty university says who exactly planted. The others answer when, where or how.
6how? The doctor explained the test results ….
How? Adverbs: clearly and patiently. The others answer when, where and how long, and a long report does not fit after results.
Stage 3b

The best Level 2 version

0/3
1
Level 1

The manager complained.

Which is the best Level 2 version?
B adds what kind, about what and when with words and phrases only. A adds a clause (that is Level 3); C and D break the word order.
2
Level 1

People visited the museum.

Which is the best Level 2 version?
A keeps the idea and adds how many, who and which museum. B loses the museum, C is a comma splice, D has no finite verb.
3
Level 1

Linh found a job.

Which is the best Level 2 version?
C adds who she is (a phrase between commas), what kind of job and where. A puts the times before the place (better: at a bank on Monday morning), B adds a clause, D breaks the word order.
Your turn

From Level 1 to Level 2

Your turn. Upgrade to Level 2: The students studied. Add who exactly, where and when.
Two models

1About thirty first-year students studied in the library until midnight.

2Two students from my class studied at a quiet café near the campus on Saturday afternoon.

Stage 4 Level 3 · Clause: add a reason or a result

Theory · Level 3, a clause
  • A clause has its own subject + verb. Level 3 adds one, most often a reason or a result; when, if and although work too.
  • 1 · and, but, so, or join two full clauses: a comma before. clause , so / , but clause The road was flooded, so the buses stopped running.
  • 2 · because, when, if, although: at the start, a comma after the clause; in the middle, usually no comma. Although the rent was high, they took the flat. · They took the flat although the rent was high.
  • 3 · however, therefore (B1+): a new sentence, or a semicolon before and a comma after. The train broke down; therefore, many passengers missed their flights.
  • , which + verb comments on the whole idea before it: The city planted thousands of trees, which made the streets cooler. It is the quickest upgrade, with little risk.
  • who / which straight after a noun says which one, with no comma: Students who arrive late cannot take the test.
  • With a comma, which after a noun only adds extra information: We met at the new library, which opens at seven.
  • Sentence types. Levels 1–2 are simple sentences; Level 3 makes them compound (…, but …) or complex (… because …). Mix the types.
  • One joining word for one link: ✗ Because it rained, so we stayed at home. ✗ Although she studied hard, but she failed.
  • A comma alone cannot join two clauses: ✗ We missed the bus, we walked to school. ✓ We missed the bus, so we walked to school.
  • From Level 2 to Level 3:
    1. Level 2 · DetailThe local factory closed its doors after forty years.
    2. Level 3 · ClauseThe local factory closed its doors after forty years, which shocked the whole town.Added:+ , which shocked the whole town a comment on the whole idea: a comma, then which + verb
  • One main idea, under about 30 words.
Stage 4a

Choose the joining word

0/8
The tag names the link. Some options carry their comma.
1reason The flight was delayed… a storm hit the airport.
A reason in the middle of the sentence: because, with no comma. when would only give the time; the tag asks for the reason.
2result Our teacher was ill… the class watched a film instead.
The illness led to the change: a result, so a comma + so.
3a comment on the whole idea Hùng passed all his exams with high marks… made his parents very proud.
After the gap there is a verb (made) but no subject: , which + verb comments on the whole first clause.
4contrast The hotel was expensive… the rooms were small and noisy.
Two facts that do not match: a comma + but.
5time Everyone stopped talking… the professor walked in.
At the moment the professor walked in: a time clause, with no comma in the middle.
6condition You will fail the course… you miss more than five classes.
It happens only in that case: if + present simple, will in the main clause.
7result The canteen started selling cheaper meals… more students now eat lunch on campus.
Cheaper meals led to the change: a result, so , so.
8reason Many young doctors leave rural hospitals… the salaries there are low.
The low pay is why they leave: because, no comma.
Stage 4b

A correct Level 3 sentence

0/4
1
Level 2

Our city banned motorbikes in the old quarter at weekends.

Which Level 3 version is correct?
B is right: the comma goes before which, never after it. A is a comma splice, C puts the comma in the wrong place, D uses two joining words, E leaves a fragment.
2
Level 2

The school closed its swimming pool.

Which Level 3 version is correct?
C: a reason in the middle, no comma. A is a comma splice, B a run-on, D has two extra commas, E cuts off a fragment.
3
Level 2

Minh applied for many jobs after graduation.

Which Level 3 version is correct?
E: Although first, then a comma. A uses although and but together, B joins with , however (a comma splice), C makes the applying the cause of the failure, D is a run-on.
4
Level 2

The company gave every worker a bonus.

Which Level 3 version is correct?
A: , which + verb after the whole idea. B is a comma splice, C has the comma after which, D uses two joining words, E puts the comment before the idea it comments on.

From Level 2 to Level 3

Your turn. Upgrade to Level 3: add a reason (because) or a result (, so / , which) to Many students in my class work part-time in cafés every evening.
Two models

1Many students in my class work part-time in cafés every evening because their parents cannot pay all their living costs.

2Many students in my class work part-time in cafés every evening, which means they often come to class tired.

Stage 5 Keep it correct: five common mistakes

Theory · five common mistakes
  • 1 · Fragment: a dependent clause or a phrase on its own. ✗ Because the bus was late. ✓ I missed the first lesson because the bus was late.
  • 2 · Run-on: two clauses with no joining word and no punctuation. ✗ The alarm rang everyone left the building. ✓ The alarm rang, and everyone left the building.
  • 3 · Comma splice: two clauses joined by a comma alone, or by , however. ✗ Walking costs nothing, it suits everyone. ✓ Walking costs nothing, and it suits everyone.
  • 4 · Subject–verb agreement: find the main subject first. ✗ The students in the new class studies on Saturdays. ✓ The students in the new class study on Saturdays.
  • 5 · Dangling phrase (dangling modifier): an opening -ing or -ed phrase must describe the subject that follows. ✗ Walking to work, the rain started. ✓ Walking to work, I got caught in the rain.
  • Also: choppy sentences (many short ones in a row: join them) and wordy ones (In my opinion, I think that …: cut the extra words).
Stage 5a

Name the mistake

0/12
Each answer is used twice.
1When the lights went out in the whole building.
A When clause alone. Add the main clause: …, the students lit candles.
2The shop was crowded, we left without buying anything.
Two clauses and only a comma: use , so or a full stop.
3The neighbours were shouting the baby could not sleep.
Two clauses with nothing between them: …shouting, so the baby …
4One of my classmates live in a village near Huế.
The main subject is One, so lives.
5Looking out of the window, the mountains were beautiful.
The mountains were not looking. Name the person: Looking out of the window, we saw …
6Because the internet was down, we called the customers by phone.
Because clause first, a comma, then the main clause: correct.
7The test was hard, however most students passed.
however cannot join with a comma: The test was hard; however, most students passed.
8Opening the letter, Lan smiled at the good news.
Lan is the one opening the letter, so the opening phrase fits its subject.
9A list of new rules for the library were put on the door.
The main subject is A list: was put.
10The factory saved energy for years it still lost money.
Two clauses, no link: …for years, but it still lost money.
11Such as rice, fish and vegetables.
No subject and no verb: We eat simple food such as …
12Tired after the night shift, the bus took the nurse home.
The bus was not tired: Tired after the night shift, the nurse took the bus home.
Stage 5b

Choose the best correction

0/4
1
Draft

The concert was cancelled, the singer was ill.

Which is the best correction?
B gives the reason with because. A is still a comma splice, C leaves a fragment, D uses two joining words and turns the reason round.
2
Draft

Having finished the report, the computer was switched off.

Which is the best correction?
Hoa finished the report, so she must be the subject after the comma: C. In A and B a break or the office finished it; D leaves a fragment.
3
Draft

The manager with her two assistants visit every branch.

Which is the best correction?
The main subject is The manager (one person), so visits; with her two assistants does not change it.
4
Draft

The city is old. It is busy. It has many temples.

These are choppy. Which is the best way to join them?
D puts the adjectives before the noun and adds with + a noun. A is a chain of comma splices, B a run-on, C two fragments.

Stage 6 Level 4 · Academic (optional, but worth a try)

Theory · Level 4, three tools
  • 1 · An action becomes a noun (nominalisation), often the subject: people use phones a lot → heavy phone use · the city grew → the growth of the city · students take part → participation · more people cycle to work → the growing popularity of cycling.
  • 2 · A careful verb (hedging): say what is likely, not what is always true. may improve · tends to reduce · is likely to increase · can lead to.
  • 3 · Strong word partners (collocations): a major cause · a serious problem · public transport · mental health · improve the quality of · reduce pollution.
  • From Level 3 to Level 4:
    1. Level 3 · ClauseMany parents give young children tablets at dinner, so the children talk less with their families.
    2. Level 4 · Academicoptional · encouragedEarly tablet use among young children tends to reduce conversation at family meals, which may slow down their language development.Added:+ Early tablet use among young children the action give children tablets becomes a noun phrase+ tends to reduce · may slow down careful verbs+ language development a common word partner
  • Keep it at B1: one noun phrase and one careful verb are enough. Do not pile up long words.
Stage 6a

Level 4 tools: nouns, careful verbs, word partners

0/8
Items 1–4: nouns. Items 5–6: careful verbs. Items 7–8: word partners.
1People exercise every day. → … improves their health.
The action exercise every day becomes the noun phrase Daily exercise, followed by a singular verb (improves).
2The government reduced taxes. → … helped small businesses.
reduced → reduction: a noun phrase can be a subject. The government reduced taxes is a whole clause and cannot be the subject as it is.
3More and more people shop online. → The … of online shopping is growing fast.
After The … of you need a noun: popular (adjective) → popularity (noun).
4Students take part in the programme for free. → … in the programme is free for students.
take part → the noun participation. A participant is a person; the gap needs the activity.
5careful Eating late at night … the risk of weight gain.
may + base verb: possible, not certain. always and will definitely claim too much; the others break the grammar.
6careful Living near a metro station … reduce travel costs.
tends to + base verb: usually true. The -ing subject is singular, so tends, and to comes before reduce.
7word partner Air pollution can have a … effect on children's lungs.
a serious effect is a usual partner; we do not say a high, much, tall or heavy effect.
8word partner Long working hours can harm workers' physical and … health.
mental health and physical health are the fixed pairs.

A correct Level 4 sentence

0/2
1
Level 3

Which Level 4 version keeps the idea and stays correct?
A turns the action into a noun phrase (Mobile payments) and uses may + base verb. B adds -s after may, C claims far too much, D has no verb.
2
Level 3

Fewer young people read books because they spend more time on social media.

Which Level 4 version keeps the idea and stays correct?
C: The rise of social media and the fall in reading are noun phrases, and is likely to keeps the claim careful. A repeats itself, B has two subjects and no verb after because, D drops to.

Know this

The ladder, level by level
  • Level 1 · Basic one short clause: subject + verb (+ object or complement).
  • Level 2 · Detail the same idea + who exactly, what kind, where, when, how often.
  • Level 3 · Clause your Level 2 + a clause with because, so, which, when, if or although.
  • Level 4 · Academicoptional · encouraged an action as a noun, a careful verb (may, tend to, is likely to) and a strong word partner.
  • Build each level on the one before it and keep the main idea.
  • Commas: before so, but and a which that comments on the whole idea; after a Because / When / If clause at the start; none before because in the middle.

Stage 8 Your ladders: two sentences of your own

Your task
  • Two ladders on common topics. Do not copy the model topics (building noise, phones in lectures).
  • Ladder A: a problem in your town or city. Ladder B: how technology helps or harms students or workers.

  • Time: about 15 minutes.
Remember: the levels
  • Level 1 · Basic one short clause: subject + verb (+ object or complement).
  • Level 2 · Detail the same idea + who exactly, what kind, where, when, how often.
  • Level 3 · Clause your Level 2 + a clause with because, so, which, when, if or although.
  • Level 4 · Academicoptional · encouraged an action as a noun, a careful verb (may, tend to, is likely to) and a strong word partner.
  • Build each level on the one before it and keep the main idea.
  • Commas: before so, but and a which that comments on the whole idea; after a Because / When / If clause at the start; none before because in the middle.

Exercise 7 · Verbs for rules — what does the rule mean?

Exercise 7

Part 1: choose the verb that makes each rule true. Part 2: read the rule in the card, then choose the sentence that means the same

Part 1 uses the SB key. Obligatory → must / have to · allowed → can · not obligatory but allowed → don’t have to · not allowed → mustn’t / can’t (SB p. 23, Ex 7 · SB p. 158 · Mai Lan Hương pp. 97–98, 101–102).

Part 1 · SB p. 23, Exercise 8 · rules of real sports

1In golf, you hit the ball into nine or eighteen holes.
the game is played that way: obligatory → have to
2Competitors argue with the referee.
arguing is against the rules → mustn’t (can’t means the same)
3In football, a goalkeeper is the only player who pick up the ball.
allowed, not obligatory → can; a goalkeeper may also kick it
4Players throw the ball backwards in rugby.
a forward pass breaks the rules, so passing backwards is obligatory → must
5A referee send a player off the pitch when he breaks the rules of the game.
the referee is allowed to; it is his decision → can
6In table tennis, the ball hit the table.
the ball = it → has to; a ball that misses the table loses the point
7In tennis, the players win every point to win a match.
you can lose some points and still win → not necessary → don’t have to

Part 2 · new rules · what do they mean?

8Sign at the pool entrance: Swimmers must shower before they get into the water.
must = obligatory (compulsory): there is no choice.
9Rule 4 of the dormitory chess league: Players don’t have to write down their moves.
don’t have to = not necessary: each player decides.
10Badminton club notice: Members can book a court up to three days ahead.
can = allowed (permitted), not obligatory.
11Notice on the climbing wall: Climbers mustn’t go above the red line without a rope.
mustn’t = not allowed (forbidden).
12Tennis club rules: Players can’t wear black-soled shoes on the courts, but they don’t have to wear white clothes.
can’t = not allowed · don’t have to = not necessary.
13The sergeant to the new cadets: ‘You have to make your bed before breakfast, and you can’t keep food in your room.’
have to = obligatory · can’t = not allowed; both are the spoken forms, natural for a sergeant talking.

Exercise 8

Choose the verb for rules that fits each gap

In the SB each verb is used once (key: 1 must · 2 have to · 3 can’t · 4 can · 5 don’t have to), but must and have to both mean obligatory, so either is marked right in gaps 1 and 2; in gap 4, must only enter one category is also good English, so must is accepted next to the SB key can. Rules: SB p. 158 · Mai Lan Hương pp. 97–98, 101–102.

Part 1 · SB p. 23, Exercise 9

The Beard and Moustache competition

Every year, over three hundred competitors enter the Beard and Moustache competition in Alaska. The rules are simple. You (1) obligatory → must; have to means the same, so both are marked right (SB key: must) be over eighteen years old and you (2) obligatory → have to (SB key); must is also marked right have a moustache or a beard, or both. Also, you (3) putting on false hair is not allowed → can’t put on false hair! In total, there are eighteen different categories, but competitors (4) allowed, but just one category → can (SB key); must only enter is also possible English, so it is marked right too only enter one category. There are categories for short beards and different moustaches, so you (5) a short beard can win too → not necessary → don’t have to have the longest moustache or the biggest beard to win a prize.

Part 2 · a new text: has to, mustn’t, can’t and the rest

The stair race at the teaching hospital

Every March, the teaching hospital next to our academy holds a stair race for charity. Runners start in the basement and climb three hundred steps to the roof of the main building. Anyone who works or studies at the hospital (6) allowed → can + base verb: no ‑s, no to enter if they want to, and every year the start list is full of nurses, porters, surgeons and cadets. Each runner (7) obligatory, and each runner = he or she → has to pay an entry fee of 100,000 dong, and the money buys new books and games for the paediatric ward. Runners (8) using a lift is against the rules → mustn’t; don’t have to would make the lift fine use the lifts, of course, and they (9) not allowed (spoken style) → can’t push past anyone on the narrow corners, because a fall on concrete stairs could be serious. You (10) going slowly is fine → not necessary → don’t have to rush: lots of people take the last few floors slowly, and every finisher gets a medal. A doctor (11) a rule from the organisers, written style → must + base verb wait at the top with oxygen and a defibrillator, just in case.

Exercise 9 · Asking about the rules — the right question

Exercise 9

The card says what the speaker wants to know: is it necessary, allowed, necessary in the past, necessary in the future? Choose the question that asks exactly that

Obligation: Do / Does … have to · permission: Can … / Am I allowed to · past: Did … have to · future: Will … have to · surprise: Don’t I have to …? (SB p. 158 · Mai Lan Hương pp. 97, 101–102). The replies give real information, the way people answer outside a classroom.
1You have just joined the badminton club. You want to know if a racket of your own is necessary.A buy my own racket?
B Not at first. The club lends rackets to beginners for the first month.
necessary or not? → Do I have to …? · Can I / Am I allowed to ask for permission, Did I have to is about the past
2You are at the pool and you would like permission to use the diving board.A Excuse me, use the diving board?
B Only after four o’clock, when a lifeguard is standing next to it.
permission → can I + base verb; do I have to / must I would ask whether diving is compulsory
3Your friend Mai has entered the photo competition. You want to know whether the rules say she must be an adult.A be eighteen or older to enter?
B Yes, and she turns eighteen in May, so she’s just in time.
do the rules oblige her? → a question about a duty: Does she have to; Can she / Is she allowed to ask about permission, Did she have to about the past
4The chess tournament has five rounds. You are on night duty on Sunday, so you hope it isn’t necessary to play them all that day.A play all five games on Sunday?
B No, players on duty can finish the last two on Monday evening.
you hope it is not necessary → ask about obligation: Do we have to …?
5Your team has only four players for a five-a-side match. You want to know if the rules let you start like that.A start the game with four?
B Yes, but the fifth player has to arrive before half-time.
do the rules let us? = permission → Can we …?; Must we / Do we have to would mean starting with four is compulsory
6An older cadet is telling you about last year’s 10 km run. You want to know if boots were compulsory then.A run in boots last year?
B Yes, full combat boots, and half the runners had blisters by the end.
compulsory in the past → Did you have to; must has no past form, and Could you asks about ability
7Next year the academy is moving its sports day to a Saturday. You want to know about a duty that starts then.A come in at the weekend?
B Only if we’re competing. Spectators can stay at home.
a duty in the future → Will we have to; must and can have no will form
8A contestant on a TV quiz show would like permission to check an answer on her phone.A use my phone to check an answer?
B Phones go in the box by the door. If you touch one, you’re out.
permission → Am I allowed to (= Can I) + base verb; the other meanings ask about a duty
9Your little sister hates running. You want to know if every race is compulsory for the children at her school sports day.A enter every race?
B No, each child picks two events, and she’s chosen the long jump and the egg-and-spoon race.
is every race compulsory? → a question about a duty: Do the children have to; Can / Could / Are … allowed to ask whether it is permitted
10A new member wants to know the time when everyone must be out of the gym.A What time leave in the evening?
B By ten. The cleaners lock the doors at a quarter past.
a time you must keep → question word + do we have to; can we would ask when leaving is allowed
11Everyone else is signing a form at the door, but the trainer has just waved you in. You are surprised.A sign in first?
B Not today. The form is only for new members.
surprise that something seems unnecessary → the negative question Don’t I have to …?; Can’t I would ask for permission

Exercise 12 · Rewrite the sentences

Exercise 12

Say the same thing in a different way: pick the ending that completes the second sentence

The first sentence is in the orange card. Only one ending keeps its meaning in correct English: a verb for rules, an ‑ing subject, good at / bored with + ‑ing, hate + ‑ing, had to · will have to.
1It isn’t necessary for guests to wear a tie at the awards dinner.→ Guests at the awards dinner.
not necessary = don’t have to; mustn’t would mean a tie is forbidden
2The rules don’t allow players to chew gum during a match.→ Players gum during a match.
not allowed = mustn’t (or can’t) + base verb
3It is obligatory for every swimmer to wear a cap in the academy pool.→ Every swimmer a cap in the academy pool.
obligatory; every swimmer = he or she → has to + base verb
4Club members are allowed to take out the club’s kayaks at weekends.→ Club members at weekends.
allowed = can + base verb
5It’s exhausting to play two matches in one afternoon.→ exhausting.
an ‑ing subject takes a singular verb: is, even though matches is plural
6Ngọc can play chess very well.→ Ngọc chess.
good at + ‑ing; well is an adverb, good an adjective
7I find training in the rain really boring.→ I in the rain.
bored (how I feel) + with + ‑ing; boring describes the training
8Tâm doesn’t like it at all when he loses, even at cards.→ Tâm , even at cards.
hate + ‑ing; Tâm = he → hates
9It was necessary for the first-year cadets to swim 200 metres in uniform.→ The first-year cadets in uniform.
must has no past form → had to + base verb (Mai Lan Hương pp. 101–102)
10Next season it will be necessary for every player to have a medical check.→ Next season, every player a medical check.
must has no future form → will have to + base verb

‑ist already means the person: cyclists
12The referee she gave us a penalty in the last minute.
→
one subject only: no she after the referee

Exercise 14 · mustn’t or don’t have to? like or would like to? — the meaning in context

Exercise 14

Read the card first: it tells you what the speaker means. Then choose the form

mustn’t = don’t do it · don’t have to = it isn’t necessary · like + ‑ing = you enjoy it in general · would like (to) = a wish, now or later (SB p. 158 · Mai Lan Hương pp. 102, 104, 109, 120).

Part 1 · mustn’t or don’t have to?

1The pharmacology test is open-book: you can use your notes and a dictionary.You memorise every drug name for it.
notes are allowed → memorising is not necessary
2A sign at the shallow end of the pool says: 1.2 m · NO DIVING.You dive here: the water isn’t deep enough.
diving here is forbidden because it is dangerous → mustn’t
3Saturday training is for the team only, but other cadets are welcome to watch.Cadets who aren’t in the team come on Saturday.
welcome to watch → not forbidden, just not necessary → don’t have to
4The match doctor thinks Phúc’s ankle might be broken.He put any weight on that foot until the X-ray.
a doctor’s order: walking on it could make it worse → mustn’t (= don’t do it!)
5Linh’s team is already through to the final, whatever happens tonight.Linh’s team win tonight’s game to reach the final.
already through → winning is not necessary; the team = it → doesn’t

Part 2 · like or would like (to)?

6Hà has played badminton every weekend since she was ten.Hà really badminton with her cousins.
a long habit she enjoys → likes + ‑ing (in general)
7Tuấn has never ridden a horse, but there is a riding school near his grandparents’ farm.Tuấn it one summer.
a wish for the future → would like to + base verb
8You are at the stadium ticket office. two tickets for the final, please.
a polite request now → I’d like + noun; I like talks about what you enjoy
9You are inviting a new classmate to the volleyball final. watch it with us on Saturday?
an invitation → Would you like to + base verb?; Do you like …? asks about habits
10Minh has just finished his first marathon and can hardly walk.Right now he a hot bath and a long sleep.
a wish at this moment → would like + noun

Exercise 16

Pick the words that say the same as the underlined part

Items 1–7 come from the article Crazy competitions! (Sheet 5, SB p. 22, Track 10), items 8–12 from Track 11, three people talking about competitive sports in schools (Sheet 6, Listening A). Exam questions rarely repeat a text word for word: they put the same idea in other words.
1… and some of them are a bit crazy!
=
a bit crazy = rather strange, said with a smile; the writer is not criticising them

=

Exercise 17 · Reading — text completion: the Wife Carrying World Championships

Exercise 17

Read the short report and choose the best option for each gap

Another crazy competition, like the ones in the SB article (the TB mentions it on SB p. 22, Exercise 4). Gaps 1–2 are one word family (Exercise 3); gaps 3–7 are verbs for rules; gaps 8–10 are ‑ing forms.

The Wife Carrying World Championships

Every summer, visitors from around the world come to Sonkajärvi, a small town in Finland, to watch one of the craziest (1) one of the + a plural noun → competitions on the sports calendar. The first race took place there in 1992, and since then (2) people who take part → competitors; to try it rules out spectators from many different countries have travelled to Sonkajärvi to try it. One local story says that a robber of the 1800s, Herkko Rosvo‑Ronkainen, trained his gang by making them run with heavy sacks on their backs.

The idea is simple: a man carries a woman along a 253.5‑metre track, and the fastest pair wins. It isn’t easy, though. On the way there are two dry obstacles and a water obstacle about one metre deep, so the carriers (3) the obstacles make it necessary; the carriers = they → have to keep their balance in the water as well as on dry ground.

The rules are short. The carrier must be at least eighteen. The woman (4) someone else’s is fine, so it is not necessary; the woman = she → doesn’t be his own wife: she (5) allowed → can + base verb be someone else’s. She must be at least seventeen and weigh at least 49 kilograms; if she weighs less, she (6) obligatory for a lighter woman; she → has to wear a rucksack with extra weight in it. Carriers (7) straps are not allowed → can’t; arms only use straps or belts to hold her; they hold her with their arms only. There is no penalty for (8) after the preposition for → dropping (double p) her, as long as the carrier picks her up again at once.

In one style, known as the ‘Estonian carry’, the woman hangs upside down on the man’s back, with her legs over his shoulders. (9) the subject of the sentence → Running + singular is like that is hard work, and the crowd loves (10) love + ‑ing it. The prize is just as unusual: the winning pair takes home the wife’s weight in drink.

Exercise 18 · Writing — the well-built sentence

Exercise 18

Each card holds a cadet’s draft: choose the version that is joined, punctuated and built correctly

The labels point to Sheet 8 (Writing · upgrading a sentence): Level 1 = a correct core, Level 3 = a joined clause, Stage 5 = the five common mistakes; the two punctuation cards go beyond Sheet 8. Each wrong version shows one trap: a comma splice, a run-on, a fragment, a wrong joining word, a missing comma or apostrophe, a missing subject or verb.
1Level 3 · result: comma + soHeavy rain flooded the courts. The organisers moved the badminton final to Sunday.→
a result → , so: a comma before so when it joins two full sentences; a comma alone is a comma splice
2Level 3 · reason: becauseMinh missed the race. He had a fever.→
a reason → because + subject + verb; because alone after a full stop is a fragment; because of + a noun
3Level 3 · contrast: comma + butBadminton looks easy. It is very tiring.→
a contrast → , but + a full clause (a subject and a verb)
4Level 3 · time: When …, + main clauseThe coach arrives. We start the warm-up.→
When + present simple , + main clause: a comma after the When clause, never will in it
5Punctuation · apostrophesthe teams captain says its the best match theyve played this year→
team’s = the captain of the team · it’s = it is · they’ve = they have; says takes no apostrophe
6Punctuation · commas in a listmy bag for the match has boots shin pads a towel and two bottles of water→
commas between the items of a list; no comma between the verb and its object
7Stage 5 · fragmentBecause the coach was ill. We had no training on Friday.→
a Because clause alone is a fragment: join it to the main clause with a comma; never because … so in one sentence
8Stage 5 · comma spliceHùng loves football, he plays every evening after dinner.→
two full sentences need a joining word (, so) or a full stop; a comma alone is a comma splice
9Level 1 · no subject: there areIn my village, are no sports clubs, so children play football in the rice fields.→
English needs a subject: there are + a plural noun; it has / have is a Vietnamese-style mistake
10Level 1 · no verbThe final very exciting, and everyone was on their feet at the end.→
every clause needs a verb: was + adjective; exciting describes the match, excited the people

Exercise 19 · Speaking — build a 7-step answer: the academy sports day

Exercise 19

Recommend one new event for the sports day: choose the sentence for each step

Situation

The academy’s sports day will add one new event this year. Class K84 must suggest one of the three.

Your class commander asks you: ‘Which event should we add, and why?’

1🪢Tug of wartwo teams of eight on one thick rope · a strip of grass · a few minutes a pull
2🏃4 × 100 m relay racefour runners and one baton per team · on the academy track · the fastest race of the day
3⚽Five-a-side football tournamentteams of five on a small pitch · short games · most of the afternoon
  • Choose one event
  • Give your main reason
  • Say why the other two suit the day less well
  • 1' prepare · 2' speak

Build the model first: for each step, pick the sentence that does that step’s job. Then hide the key and give your own answer, about the same event or another one.

Point
Point: the recommendation in a few words.
Why
Why: the main reason: anyone can help the team, not only the best athletes.
How
How: how the event would work on the day: what it needs, who pulls, who wins.
Example
Example: one real pull at one school, with one detail (the small class and the captain’s shouts).
Result
Result: what changed for those same classmates afterwards.
Limitation
Limitation: Admittedly …, but … admits a weak point of the tug of war, then answers it.
Evaluation
Evaluation: a final judgement from a new angle (what a sports day is for), not the Point again.
Model answer

PointIf we can only add one event, I'd go for the tug of war. WhyMainly because it's the one event where almost anybody can help their team, so cadets who'd never get picked for a relay or a football side would still get a real chance to compete. HowAll it needs is a thick rope and a strip of grass: each class puts up a team of eight, and the side that drags the middle of the rope over its own line wins the pull. ExampleWe had one every New Year at my secondary school, and I still remember our class, with nobody tall or strong in it, beating a much bigger class because we leaned back and pulled every time our captain shouted. ResultFor weeks after that, even classmates who'd always hated PE kept asking when we could have another go. LimitationAdmittedly, a pull is over in a minute or two, and people can hurt their hands or backs if nobody shows them how to hold the rope, but a ten-minute talk from the PE staff before the first round would sort that out. EvaluationOn balance, a sports day should get the whole class out on the field, not just the four fastest runners or the five best footballers, and the tug of war does that better than anything else on the list.

2:00

Exercise 20

Complete the notice: choose the best option for each gap

Gaps 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 are verbs for rules (a written notice prefers must / mustn’t, SB p. 158); gaps 3, 6 and 10 are ‑ing forms. Homework (Day 7 of the 1‑3‑7 plan, Sheet 10): eight rules for a crazy competition of your own, with at least four different verbs for rules.

The K84 Charity Fun Run · rules for runners

5 km round the academy · start 6.30 a.m. at the main gate · all the money raised buys wheelchairs for the rehabilitation centre

Every runner (1) a written notice → must + base verb (the formal style, SB p. 158) register at the desk by 6.15 and collect a running number. You (2) walking the whole way is fine, so being an athlete is not necessary be an athlete to take part: plenty of people walk the whole way with friends. (3) the subject → Running + singular is with headphones is not allowed, because you need to hear the marshals. Runners (4) leaving the route is against the rules → mustn’t leave the marked route, even if they know a quicker way.

Cadets (5) allowed → can; uniform isn’t needed run in sports kit; nobody needs to wear uniform. If you feel unwell, go to one of the first-aid points: nobody will laugh at you for (6) after the preposition for → asking for help. Teenagers under sixteen (7) obligatory, and teenagers is plural → have to bring a form signed by a parent. The entry fee is 50,000 dong, but a runner who collects more than a million dong from sponsors (8) not necessary for a runner who raised the money; he or she → doesn’t pay it.

Q (9) asking for permission → Can I + base verb? run with my dog? A Sorry, no animals on the course.

Thank you for (10) thank you for + ‑ing the rehabilitation centre, and enjoy the run!

Which verb does the rule need?
3′

Pick the verb for each rule, then press Check. Ask yourself: is it obligatory, allowed, not necessary or not allowed?

1In volleyball, players catch the ball; they have to hit it cleanly.
Catching the ball is a fault, so it is not allowed: can’t.
2Amateurs are welcome in the Sunday 10 km race in the park; runners belong to a club.
Club membership is not necessary, but nobody stops you joining one: don’t have to.
3In basketball, a team take a shot within 24 seconds of getting the ball.
The shot clock makes it obligatory: has to (one team, so has).
4Swimmers in a backstroke race start in the water, not from the blocks.
There is no choice in the rules: have to.
5In judo, you punch or kick your opponent; it’s a sport of throws and holds.
Punching is forbidden, not just unnecessary: mustn’t.
6In tennis you serve underarm if you want to; it’s unusual, but it’s allowed.
if you want to … it’s allowed: a choice, so can.
7Visitors to the academy’s sports day bring their own chairs; there are benches all along the track.
Bringing a chair is fine but not needed: don’t have to.
8A boxer hit his opponent below the belt.
A blow below the belt breaks the rules: mustn’t.
9In a relay race, each runner pass the baton inside the changeover zone.
A pass outside the zone means disqualification, so it is obligatory: has to.
10Golfers carry their own clubs; most professionals pay a caddie to do it.
Someone else may carry them, so it is not necessary: don’t have to.

Pairs that look alike

GoalChoose between competition and rule words that look or mean alike, and give a reason for each choice.
2a
Compare the pairs

Read both sides of each card, then cover them and try the quick test.

win · beat
win /wɪn/
you win a thing: a match, a race, a medal, a prize, the cup
Linh won the women’s 800 metres at the academy sports day by almost a second.
beat /biːt/
you beat people: another runner, another player, the other side
She beat the runner from the nursing faculty, who had won the race two years in a row.
✗ My little sister won me at table tennis for the first time last night. (→ beat)
a race · a match
a race /ə reɪs/
everyone goes from a start to a finish line, and the fastest wins
The 10 km race starts at the north gate and finishes in front of the library.
a match /ə mætʃ/
one side against another, player v player or team v team; the score decides
The basketball match went into extra time after a shot on the final buzzer.
✗ Did you watch the Formula 1 match on Sunday afternoon? (→ race)
a competitor · a competition · competitive
a competitor /ə kəmˈpetɪtə(r)/
a person who takes part
Competitors in the bike race get a free drink at every checkpoint.
a competition /ə ˌkɒmpəˈtɪʃn/
the event itself
The quiz competition on Teachers’ Day is open to every class in the academy.
competitive /kəmˈpetətɪv/
adjective: keen to win, or (a sport) with winners and losers
Our Friday football starts friendly and gets more competitive every minute.
✗ More than two hundred competitions took part in the sea swim. (→ competitors)
a spectator · an audience
a spectator /ə spekˈteɪtə(r)/
a person watching a sports event, usually there in person
The spectators stood and clapped as the last runner crossed the line.
an audience /ən ˈɔːdiəns/
the whole group watching a show, a film, a concert or a talk
The audience in the lecture hall went quiet when the professor showed the X-ray.
✗ The audience at the stadium booed the referee after the penalty. (→ spectators, or the crowd)
a goal · a point
a goal /ə ɡəʊl/
the ball goes into a net or between posts: football, handball, hockey
Mai scored the only goal of the match with a header in the last minute.
a point /ə pɔɪnt/
a unit of score in badminton, tennis, volleyball and basketball
We lost the first point of the game, then won the next six in a row.
✗ Lan scored three goals in a row in the second game of the badminton final. (→ won three points)
mustn’t · don’t have to
mustn’t /ˈmʌsnt/
it isn’t allowed: don’t do it!
Spectators mustn’t walk across the track while a race is on.
don’t have to /dəʊnt ˈhæf tə/
there’s no need, but nobody stops you
You don’t have to sign up in advance for the running track; it’s open to everyone at weekends.
✗ Lunch is included in the price, so competitors mustn’t bring their own food. (→ don’t have to)
must · have to
must /mʌst/
obligatory; often the speaker’s own rule, or a formal written notice
‘I must start going to bed before midnight,’ Quân told us after falling asleep in anatomy.
have to /ˈhæf tə/
obligatory; usually a rule that comes from outside (a coach, a club, a law); past: had to
In our dormitory, we have to switch the lights off at eleven, whether we’ve finished studying or not.
✗ Last Saturday we must run ten kilometres before breakfast. (→ had to)
argue with · argue about
argue with /ˈɑːɡjuː wɪð/
with + the person you disagree with
Hùng loves arguing with our PE teacher about the rules of handball.
argue about /ˈɑːɡjuː əˈbaʊt/
about + the thing you disagree on
The two coaches argued about the result for twenty minutes after the race.
✗ Our number 9 argued the referee about every free kick. (→ argued with)
2b
Which one, and why?
7′
1 · Đức trained for months, and in the end he ____ his older brother in the 10 km race.
beat: the object is a person. We win a race or a cup, and we score goals or points.
2 · The 1,500 metres freestyle is the longest ____ in Olympic pool swimming.
race: everyone swims from start to finish and the fastest wins. A match is one side against another, and a competitor is a person.
3 · Over a hundred ____ jumped into the lake when the starting gun fired.
competitors: people jump into a lake. Competitions are events, and competitive is an adjective.
4 · The ____ in the stadium went silent when the captain fell and didn’t get up.
spectators: people watching sport in the stadium. An audience watches a show, and viewers watch on a screen.
5 · In our dormitory league, players ____ wear matching shirts; any colour will do.
don’t have to: matching shirts aren’t necessary. Mustn’t and can’t would mean they are forbidden.
6 · Players ____ wear rings or earrings during a football match; jewellery can injure someone.
mustn’t: the reason given (it can injure someone) shows the rule forbids it.
7 · Nurses on the night shift ____ check every patient once an hour.
have to: the subject is plural (nurses), so have, not has; must never takes to.
8 · In badminton, you win a ____ every time the shuttle hits the floor on your opponent’s side.
point: every rally in badminton ends with a point. A goal needs a net or posts, and a score is the total, not one unit.

Fix the sentence
5′

Each underlined part is wrong. Pick the correct version from the list.

1The organisers say every runner must to carry a bottle of water on the mountain section.
→
Must takes the verb without to: must carry. (Has to would also work; have to is wrong after every runner.)
2A substitute doesn’t can come onto the pitch until the referee waves him on.
→
Can never uses do or does: the negative is can’t (cannot).
3Do I must register before Friday, or can I sign up on the day?
→
Must never takes do. The natural spoken question is Do I have to …? (Must I …? exists, but it sounds formal.)
4Cadets mustn’t pay for swimming lessons at the academy pool; they’re free.
→
Paying isn’t forbidden, only unnecessary: don’t have to. Mustn’t means “it isn’t allowed”.
5Nobody expected a first-year cadet to win the defending champion in the chess final.
→
The object is a person, so beat. We win a game, a final or a title; win over means “persuade”.
6At the finish, a medical team checked the heart rate of every competition.
→
Hearts belong to people: a person who takes part is a competitor; after every, singular.
7Ten thousand audiences watched the final from the stands.
→
People in the stands at a sports event are spectators. Audience means a whole group at a show, so never “ten thousand audiences”.
8The mountain race has a limited time of four hours, so slower runners set off first.
→
The fixed phrase is a time limit: the most time you are allowed.
9In futsal, outfield players don’t allowed to touch the ball with their hands.
→
Allowed works with be: players aren’t allowed to …
10Two players were sent out for fighting in the second half.
→
In sport, a player who must leave the pitch is sent off (past participle sent, particle off).

Complete Tuấn’s post about the Mop Race
5′

The Mop Race: the rules for this year

Every December, the cadets on the third floor of our dormitory hold the craziest competition in the academy: the Mop Race. Teams (1) plural subject (Teams): have to; must never takes to be made up of four people. One person sits on a big floor cloth, and the other three pull him down the corridor with a rope. Teams (2) a free choice the rules allow: can dress their rider in any costume they like, and last year the winners turned theirs into a tiny ambulance with a red cross. You (3) finishing first is not necessary for the costume prize: don’t have to finish first to take home a prize, because there’s one for the best costume as well. There are a few strict rules, though. The rider (4) holding on is forbidden, and there is a penalty: mustn’t hold on to the walls, and if he falls off the cloth, his team goes back to the start. Each race has a (5) the fixed phrase: a time limit of ninety seconds, and a fifth-year student acts as the (6) the person with the whistle who controls the race: the referee, with a whistle and a very serious face. Anyone who argues with him is out!

In my favourite sport, you have to … but you don’t have to …

Examples

1In my favourite sport, volleyball, you have to move round one position each time your team wins back the serve, but once the ball is in play, you don’t have to stay in your own spot; players can move anywhere on their side of the net.

1The craziest competition I’d love to enter is a mud race. You have to crawl under nets and climb over walls, and after ten minutes you can’t tell one runner from another.

2The craziest competition I’d love to enter is a pillow fight tournament. You can hit as hard as you like, but you mustn’t aim at anyone’s face.

Upgrade my answer
8′
Speaking task · a 20-second explanation

‘Tell me about a game you and your friends play. What are two of its rules?’

Speak for about 20 seconds with Tier 1 words and have to, can’t and don’t have to: the game, two rules and what happens to someone who breaks one.

Example

After dinner my roommates and I play đá cầu in the yard behind the dormitory. The shuttlecock has to stay in the air, and nobody can use their hands. You don’t have to pass to anyone in particular; you just kick it to whoever is closest. Whoever lets it drop is out.

Now go through the 7-step frame and add two Tier 2 chunks, one short sentence per step.

Example

PointThe game my roommates and I play most is đá cầu, and it really comes down to two rules. WhyThose two rules keep the game fast, and they stop it turning into an argument. HowYou have to keep it off the ground with your feet, knees or head, and you can’t touch it with your hands or arms. ExampleLast Sunday Minh caught it on reflex when it flew at his face, so he broke the rules and had to sit out the next round. ResultWe all laughed, but nobody complained, because in our group everyone follows the rules. LimitationWe don’t have a referee, of course, so now and then two people can’t agree whether it touched the ground. EvaluationEven so, a game this simple is perfect for a ten-minute break between study sessions.

Choose a follow-up question and give a 20-second answer.

  • Do games between friends need a referee?
  • Which is more fun: a game with strict rules or one with almost none?
Example

Not really. Among friends, everybody knows the rules, and a bit of arguing is part of the fun. But if there’s a prize, even just a bottle of iced tea, I’d want someone neutral watching.

Read the model and spot all seven steps.

PointThe game I play most with friends is cờ tướng, or Chinese chess, and two of its rules decide almost every game. WhyThat’s because they limit what the two most important pieces can do. HowYour general has to stay inside his palace, a small square of nine points, and your elephants can’t cross the river into the other half of the board. ExampleFor example, last weekend my roommate Quân trapped my general in a corner of the palace, and because it wasn’t allowed to step outside, I lost in eleven moves. ResultAs a result, I now protect my general long before the attack comes, which has made me a much more careful player. LimitationAdmittedly, these rules make the game feel slow at first, and new players often ask why the general can’t just run away. EvaluationEven so, a beginner doesn’t have to study openings for years to enjoy it, and those two rules are exactly what turn a simple race to the other side into a real battle of plans.

Cover the model and explain your own game again in 60–90 seconds, taking it through all seven steps.

New situation · explain the Wheelbarrow Race to visitors
10′
Task · speak for 45–60 seconds

On the academy’s open day, a group of high-school students stops at your stand. Your platoon runs the Wheelbarrow Race, and they want to know how it works before they have a go. These are the notes on your organiser’s card.

  • pairs · the ‘wheelbarrow’ walks on his hands · the ‘pusher’ holds his ankles
  • course: 20 m to a cone and back
  • change roles at the cone
  • pusher lets go of the ankles → start that half again
  • gloves: allowed · shoes: not necessary
  • time limit: 2 minutes · slower → out
  1. Explain the race in 45–60 seconds with at least four different verbs for rules.
  2. Answer one student’s question: Do we have to be strong to win?
1:00Tap every chunk you use.
🚀 Challenge card

Do at least two:

  • use both mustn’t (not allowed) and don’t have to (not necessary)
  • say what happens when a pair breaks a rule: If …, they have to …
  • use one Tier 2 chunk (break the rules, a time limit, cross the finish line)
  • use had to or will have to once
Suggested answers · 3 levels
● Core

The rulesIn the Wheelbarrow Race you work in pairs. One person walks on his hands, and the other holds his ankles. You have to go to the cone and back, and you change places at the cone. The pusher mustn’t let go. You can wear gloves if you like.

The questionNo, not really. The course is only twenty metres each way, so it’s over very quickly.

●● Stretch

The rulesIt’s a race for pairs. One of you is the ‘wheelbarrow’ and walks on your hands, while your partner holds your ankles and pushes. You have to swap roles at the cone halfway, and if the pusher lets go, you have to start that half again. Gloves are allowed, and you don’t have to keep your shoes on. There’s a time limit of two minutes, so keep moving!

The questionNot really. Last year’s winners were the smallest pair in the race, but they never once fell over.

●●● Challenge

The rulesIt looks silly, but it’s harder than it seems. One partner walks on his hands while the other holds his ankles, and together you have to reach the cone twenty metres away, swap roles and come back. The pusher mustn’t let go at any point, because if he does, the pair goes back and does that half again. You can wear gloves, but nobody can start early. Any pair that hasn’t crossed the finish line after two minutes is out, so agree on a rhythm before you start.

The questionStrength helps, but it isn’t everything. Last year two first-year girls beat a pair of much bigger fifth-year students, because they kept a steady rhythm and never had to go back.

-ing or to + verb?

Pick the form for each gap, then press Check. Look at the word just before the gap (a verb, a preposition, a modal) or at the start of the sentence.

1Do you enjoy football on TV, or would you rather play it yourself?
enjoy + ‑ing: enjoy watching. Enjoy is never followed by to.
2After losing the semi-final, our captain decided twice a week instead of once.
decide + to + verb: decided to train.
3 in front of a big crowd makes my hands shake.

4Thảo is famous for jokes in the changing room before every match.
After a preposition (for), the ‑ing form: famous for telling.

7The physio says I can jogging again next week.
After a modal verb (can), the base form: can start.
8After scoring an own goal last week, our defender is afraid of the ball near his own net.
After the preposition of: touching.
9I hope a place in the academy’s volleyball team this year.
hope + to + verb: hope to win.
10Instead of the referee, our captain shook his hand and walked away.
Instead of is a preposition, so the ‑ing form follows.
